full_judgment:
Obaidul Hassan J. Both the Civil Appeals and the Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal involving similar question of laws and almost identical facts and the suit land as well as the parties in those cases are same having been heard together are now being disposed of by this common judgment. 

2. Both the Civil Appeals No.70-71 of 2012 by leave granting order dated 15.04.2012 in Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal (CPLA) No.642 of 2009 and 684 of 2009 respectively and the Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal (CPLA) No.2001 of 2021 are directed against the judgment and order dated 14.01.2009 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.1302 of 2003 heard analogously with Civil Revision No.1303 of 2003 making the Rules absolute reversing the judgment and order dated 18.02.2003 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Noakhali allowing Miscellaneous Appeal No.60 of 2001 preferred by the preemptors and disallowing the Miscellaneous Appeal No.51 of 2001 preferred by the co-preemptor and Miscellaneous Appeal N0.58 of 2001 preferred by the pre-emptees thereby reversed the judgment and order dated 15.05.2001 passed by the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Begumganj, Noakhali in Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No.17 of 1999 allowing the pre-emption case to the extent of 18 decimals land in favour of the preemptors and the rest 18 decimals land in favour of the co-preemptor. 

3. The relevant facts necessary for the disposal of the Civil Appeals No.70-71 of 2012 and the Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal (CPLA) No.2001 of 2021 are that on 01.04.1999 the appellants in Civil Appeal No.70 of 2012 as petitioners filed Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No.17 of 1999 in the Court of Senior Assistant 
Judge, Begumganj, Noakhali under Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 for pre-emption of 36 decimals land as appended to the pre-emption petition. The petitioners' case, in a nutshell, is that the opposite party No.5, Sayed Noor Nabi in the pre-emption case having owned and possessed the case land appertaining to plot No.7981 transferred the same to pre-emptees-opposite parties No.1-4 secretly by registered Kabala No.10466 dated 26.10.1997 which was registered on 03.12.1998. The pre-emptees-opposite parties No.1-4 are neither co-sharer tenants of the holding nor contiguous land holders but they are mere stranger purchasers. Their further case is that the preemptors purchased 20 decimals land in plot No.7980 situated contiguous east to the case plot by registered Sale Deed No.10999 dated 07.12.1978 from Mohammad Ullah and others. The pre-emptors also purchased 131/3 decimal lands of plot No.7980 from the said Mohammad Ullah and others by registered Sale Deed No.10993 dated 08.12.1978. Thus, the preemptors became the owners of total 33'/2decimals land in plot No.7980. Again, they purchased TA decimals land of plot No.8354 situated contiguous north of the case plot from Lalmoti Begum by registered Sale Deed dated 12.01.1991. The vendee No.2 of the said deed is the wife of preemptor No.1 and is benamdar of him, thus she is impleaded as opposite party No.6. They are contiguous land holders of the disputed land. The case land being contiguous to their homestead is very essential for them. The pre-emtees-opposite parties No. 1-4 purchased the case land without any knowledge of the preemptors. They did never take over the possession of the case land. The preemptors came to know about the alleged sale deed in the last part of Falgoon 1405 B.S. while the pre-emptees-opposite parties No.1-4 were filling up the lower part of the case land excavating soil from the nearby canal. Thereafter, on receipt of the certified copy of the alleged Kabala on 23.03.1999 the pre-emptors came to know about the alleged transfer properly and filed the present case. 

4. The preemptees-opposite parties No.1-4 contested the case by filing a written objection contending, inter alia, that the case is bad for non-joinder of necessary parties, the case is barred by limitation and the case is barred by the principle of estoppels, waiver and acquiescence. Their case, in brief, is that the case land originally belonged to Upendra Kumar Bhoumik and Manindra Kumar Bhoumik. Subsequently, Manindra Kumar Bhoumik became the owner of the case land measuring 36 decimal through family amicable settlement. Later on, he transferred the said land to the opposite party No.5 by a sale deed. Thereafter, the opposite party No.5 transferred the case land to the opposite parties No.1-4 by Sale Deed No.10466 dated 26.10.1997 within the very knowledge of the preemptors. Prior to the said transfer the vendor-opposite party No.5 had asked all the co-sharer tenants and the tenants holding land contiguous to the case land whether they would purchase the case land but all of them had denied to purchase the same. The opposite parties No.1-4 purchased the case land for the purpose of construction of a dwelling house and after purchase they had made improvement work thereon spending of Tk.1,25,000.00. The preemptors are not entitled to pre-empt the case land and as such the pre-emption case is liable to be rejected. 

5. The respondent No.1 was impleaded as opposite party No.23 in the Pre-emption Case. He filed an application on 24.06.1999 to be a co-preemptor under Section 96(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act claiming that on 04.04.1999 summons was not served on him as per provision of Order V Rule 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The trial Court by order dated 24.06.1999 summarily rejected the said application with the observation that the date of knowledge had not been mentioned in the said application and the period of limitation for filing pre-emption case against the alleged sale deed also expired on 02.04.1999. 

6. Subsequently, the opposite party No.23-respondent No. I filed another application on 07.07.1999 under Section 96(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act read with Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure stating that he is a co-sharer by inheritance in the case holding. He had been staying in Chattogram for long and he used to run a grocery shop there. After coming to visit his native's home at Noakhali on 20.06.1999 he came to know about the preemption proceeding and alleged transfer from his brother Nurul Huda, who is opposite party No.21 in the pre-emption case. He obtained the copy of pre-emption case or. 22.06.1999 and earlier he filed an application for adding him as co-preemptor on 24.06.1999 Within two months from the date of said knowledge. Since the date of his knowledge about the alleged transfer was not mentioned in the said application, the same was rejected on ground of limitation. The opposite party No.23 could not know about the alleged transfer due to the fraudulent activities of the opposite parties No.1-5. No summon had been served on the opposite party No.23 at all. According to law, the application for adding as co-preemptor must be filed within two months from the date of knowledge and accordingly the opposite party No.23 filed the said application within two months from the date of knowledge. The trial Court stated that the report of the process-server regarding summons was not found on the record. The opposite party No.23 prayed for review of the earlier order dated 24.06.1999 and to treat the application dated 07.07.1999 as one filed under Section 96(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. 

7. The pre-emptors filed a written objection on 25.07.1999 against the said application dated 07.07.1999 filed by the opposite party No.23 contending that earlier on 24.06.1999 similar application was rejected on merit on ground of limitation. The opposite party No.23 was all along informed about the alleged transfer. The opposite them are neighbor to each other. Particularly, the opposite party No.21 is the brother of opposite party No.23 and the opposite party No.18 is one of the witnesses of the alleged sale deed. The opposite party No.18 married off her daughter Tajnahar Begum with the son of Daliler Rahman, who is a neighbor of the opposite parties No.1-4. The summons on the opposite party No.23 was served on 04.04.1999. The said order is not liable to be reviewed as well as a fresh application on the same cause of action is not maintainable beyond the period of limitation prescribed by law. The opposite party No.23 was set as co-petitioner to serve the purpose of the opposite parties No.1-4- pre-emptees and he had knowledge about the transfer through his brothers who were opposite parties No.18 and 21. 

8. The opposite parties No.1-4-preemptees also filed a written objection against the said application dated 07.07.1999 contending, inter alia, that the disputed transfer and delivery of possession of the case land in their favour was made within the knowledge of pre-emptors. Before the said transfer of the case land, the vendor has offered the same to the pre-emptors and all other co-sharers and contiguous landowners but they refused to purchase. After purchase of the case land the pre-emptees made improvement works by spending about Tk.1,25,000.00 and as such the applications dated 24.06.1999 and 07.07.1999 are liable to be rejected. 

9. After hearing the parties the trial Court by its order dated 09.08.1999 admitted the application dated 07.07.1999 for the time being subject to hearing the same on merit at the time of final hearing of the case and directed the opposite party No.23 to deposit the requisite pre-emption money as per law. 

10. The trial court on completion of the trial allowed the preemption case to the extent of 18 decimals land in favour of the pre-emptors and the rest 18 decimals land in favour of the opposite party No.23-co-preemptor by judgment and order dated 15.05.2001. Being aggrieved with the judgment and order dated 15.05.2001 passed by the trial Court the pre-emptors preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No.60 of 2001 while the co-pre-emptor preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No.51 of 2001 and the opposite parties No.1-4- pre-emptees flied Miscellaneous Appeal No.58 of 2001 in the Court of the District Judge, Noakhali. The aforesaid three appeals were eventually transferred to the Court of Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Noakhali for final hearing. Upon analogous hearing of those appeals, the appellate Court below vide judgment and order dated 18.02.2003 allowed Miscellaneous Appeal No.60 of 2001 preferred by the pre-emptors reversing the judgment of the trial Court thereby allowed the Miscellaneous Case No.17 of 1999 in full in favour of the pre-emptors and disallowed other two appeals. 

11. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and order dated 18.02.2003 passed by the appellate Court below in Miscellaneous Appeal No.60 of 2001, the co-preemptor filed Civil Revision No.1302 of 2003 while against the judgment and order passed by the appellate Court below in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 51 of 2001 he filed Civil Revision No.1303 of 2003 before the High Court Division. The High Court Division upon analogous hearing was pleased to make the Rules absolute in both the Civil Revisions by judgment and order dated 14.01.2009 reversing the judgment and order dated 18.02.2003 passed by the appellate Court below and restored the judgment and order of the trial Court.
 
12. Being dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and order dated 14.01.2009 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.1303 of 2003 the co-preemptor filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.684 of 2009 and preemptors filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.2001 of 2021 before this Division while against the impugned judgment and order dated 14.01.2009 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.1302 of 2003 the preemptors filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.642 of 2009 before this Division. Both the Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal No.642 and 684 of 2009 were heard by this Division analogously and upon hearing leave was granted in both the Civil Petitions by order dated 15.04.2012. Therefore, Civil Appeal No.70 of 2012 arose out of Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.642 of 2009 while Civil Appeal No.71 of 2012 arose out of Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.684 of 2009. 

13. Mr. Khair Ezaz Maswood, learned senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants and petitioners in Civil Appeal No.70 and Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.2001 of 2021 and also on behalf of the respondents in Civil Appeal No.71 of 2012 taking us through the impugned judgment and order dated 14.01.2009 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.1303 of 2003 heard along with Civil Revision No.1302 of 2003, judgments and orders of the appellate Court below as well as the trial Court and other materials on record, contends that the High Court Division has committed illegality in totally misconceiving the case of the appellant upon mis-reading and misconstruing the evidence and materials on record and thereby mis-directed beyond the law and facts of the case in passing the erroneous judgment occasioning serious miscarriage of justice and as such the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside. The learned senior Counsel contends next that the High Court Division erred in law in not taking into account of the fact that the application of the co-preemptor was filed beyond the time prescribed under Section 96(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and as such the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is liable to be set aside. The learned senior Counsel contends next that the High Court Division committed error of law in not considering that from the evidence of the P.W.1, P.W.4 and 0.P.W.1 along with the certificate of the local Union Parishad (Exhibit-4) it is proved beyond doubt that summons in the Preemption Case was served on 04.04.1999. But the co-preemptor filed the application on 24.06.1999 which is not within two months from the service of summons on him, therefore, the application filed by the co-preemptor for adding him as co-preemptor is barred by limitation. The leaned senior Counsel submits lastly that the High Court Division committed error of law in reversing the judgment of the appellate Court below venturing into fresh assessment of evidence beyond its scope in revisional jurisdiction and failed to consider that on material issue both the Courts of facts concurred while disbelieving the co-pre-emptor's statement of knowledge within the purview of Section 96(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, there-fore the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division warrants interference by this Division. 

14. On the contrary, Mr. Sk. Md. Morshed, learned senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant in Civil Appeal No.71 of 2012 strenuously opposes the submissions put forth on behalf of the appellants in Civil Appeal No.70 of 2012 and Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.2001 of 2021. The learned Counsel argues that the High Court Division has committed illegality in allowing the pre-emption in favour of the co-preemptor only to the extent of half portion of the case land and also allowing remaining half portion of the case land in favour of the pre-emptors while admittedly the co-pre-emptor being a co-sharer by inheritance will get priority over the preemptors in getting the case land by way of pre-emption whereas the preemptors are the contiguous land holders. The learned senior Counsel contends next that although the High Court Division rightly found that the application by the co-preemptor is not time barred and he is a co-sharer by inheritance but the High Court Division contradictorily observed that the co-preemptor would get only half of the case land, hence, impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is not tenable in the eye of law. Because according to the provisions of law the co-preemptor being a co-sharer by inheritance and his application being filed within two months from the date of knowledge he should have been allowed the pre-emption of entire case land. The learned Counsel contends next that the High Court Division upon restoring the judgment and order of the trial Court most illegally allowed the pre-emptors and co-preemptor in equal portion of the case land and as such the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division calls for interference by this Division. 

15. Mr. Zulfiqur Bulbul Chowdhury, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents in Civil Appeal No.70 of 2012 almost adopted the submissions of the learned senior Counsel for the appellants in Civil Appeal No.71 of 2012. The learned Counsel additionally argues that in view of the deposition of 0.P. W.1 and O.P.W.2 together with Exhibits-8 and 9 it is clear that the co-preemptor used to stay in Chattogram for the purpose of his business and he came to the home at Eklashpur, Noakhali occasionally which further lends support to the fact that the summons was not served on the co-pre-emptor properly and the co-preemptor learnt about the alleged transfer on 20.06.1999 from the opposite party No.21. Therefore, the application filed by the co-preemptor is not barred by limitation, but the appellate Court below most illegally found that the application of the co-pre-emptor is not maintainable being barred by limitation. The co-preemptor will get priority over the preemptees in getting the case land and as such the Civil Appeal No.70 of 2012 is liable to be dismissed. 

16. We have perused the judgment and order dated 14.01.2009 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revisions No.1302-1303 of 2003. We have also considered the submissions of the learned Counsels for the respective parties and gone through the judgments and orders of the appellate Court below as well as the trial Court, evidences and other materials on record. 

17. It is undisputed that the preemptors are the contiguous land owners of the case holding while the co-preemptor is a co-sharer by inheritance in the case holding. Now a pertinent question arises as to which category between a co-sharer by inheritance and a tenant having the contiguous land will get primacy in getting the case land by way of pre-emption. In this regard, the appellate Court below rightly formulated a question for taking proper decision nevertheless finally it arrived at a wrong decision. 

18. The appellate Court below observed the following: 
"The main contention in the appeal is that whether the claim of the co-petitioner Abul Kashem is barred under Section 96(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and if the answer is "no" then whether the original pre-emptors' claim of pre-emption subsists as contiguous landholder inpresence of co-preemptor who appears to be a co-sharer by inheritance in the case holding." 

19. Prior to the amendment in the year 2006, Section 96(5) of . the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (hereinafter referred to as SAT Act, 1950) provides for three types of persons for seeking pre-emption and lays down the order of priority among those three types. By referring Sub-section (5) of Section 96 this Division in the case of Md. Azimuddin Pramanik & others Vs. Sree Satya Narayan Pramanik & others, reported in 37 DLR(AD) (1985) 220 most candidly observed as follows: 
"2  This distinction between a co-sharer tenant and a tenant having the contiguous land has been again pro-nounced in definite terms and language in sub-section (5). This sub-section has set forth the prior rights to purchase under section 96. It is quoted below: 
(5) (a). If (i) a co-sharer tenant whose interest has accrued by inheritance and (ii) a co-sharer tenant whose interest has accrued by purchase and (iii) a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred apply under this section and comply with the provisions herein contained, the applicant or applicants shall have the prior right to purchase under this section in the order in which they have been mentioned above. 
As appears clearly from sub-section 5(i)(a) a co-sharer by inheritance gets the first priority and if he claims per-emption he will exclude all other claimants. If a co-sharer by purchase claims preemption, the claim of a contiguous land-holder stands superseded. Now in the instant case, the co-sharers by purchase already purchased the land, and no other co-sharer has come forward claiming pre-emption........”
 
20. It is palpably clear from the above that prior to the enactment of State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 2006 under Section 96 of SAT Act, 1950 the following categories of persons were entitled to claim pre-emption, viz. (i) a co-sharer tenant whose interest has accrued by inheritance and (ii) a co-sharer tenant whose interest has accrued by purchase and (iii) a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred. Among the afore-said three categories the first category always excludes the other two categories and in absence of the first category, the second category excludes the third category. 

21. In the case in hand, the preemption was initially sought by the preemptors, who are contiguous land owners while a co-applicant sought for pre-emption is a co-sharer tenant by inheritance in the case holding. Given the said backdrop the only question arises as to who will be entitled to get the case land by way of pre-emption between the co-applicant and the original preemptors. The question is also fairly answered by this Division in the case of Chan Miah Vs. Md. Dabirul Islam Khan and Ors., reported in 8 MLR(AD) 310 observed the following: 
"9. Section 96(6)(b) thereof provides that if the Court finds that the applications of more than one applicant have to be allowed, it shall apportion the amount which each allowed applicant has to deposit and fix a reasonable time within which such deposit has to be made. Failure by any one allowed applicant to deposit the required sum within the time fixed shall make his application liable to be dismissed. 
10. But the situation would be different if there is only one applicant of the group having priority over the pre-emptor, then the applicant who is a co-sharer by inheritance steps into the shoes of the pre-emptor and both the provision of sections 96(4) and 6(b) of the Act are applicable in the case of the applicant and it would not be an illegality to order him to deposit the consideration money together with the compensation prior to the determination of the issues as to limitation and co-sharership i.e., prior to the decision in the case either allowing or rejecting the pre-emption or the application of the co-applicant on the ground of bar of limitation and/or being a co-sharer. Though under the law a co-applicant is entitled to get a share corresponding to his interest in the raiyati holding as compared to that of the other co-sharer applicants in a case where there are competing co-applicants of the same groups and the Court is to determine the same, but the situation is otherwise when only one applicant with priority over the pre-emptor seeks for preempting the case holding. 
11. In the instant case, prima fade, upon assertion of me applicant-petitioner that he is the co-sharer by inheritance if found to be true having undoubtedly a prior claim over the pre-emptor who is admittedly a co-sharer by contiguity and there being no other claimant-applicant to pre-empt the case land  " 

22. It is transparent from the aforesaid observation that in a situation when the preemptor is a co-sharer tenant in the contiguous land and the co-petitioner is a co-sharer by inheritance, the co-petitioner being a co-sharer by inheritance must get priority over the pre-emptor who is a co-sharer tenant in the contiguous land, thus the said co-petitioner steps into the shoes of the pre-emptor. In view of the above position of law, although the opposite party No.23appellant in Civil Appeal No.71 of 2012 was the co-petitioner but he being a co-sharer by inheritance is exclusively entitled to get the entire case land by way of pre-emption excluding the pre-emptors who were co-sharers tenants in the contiguous land. 

23. At this juncture, we need to examine whether the co-petitioner has filed the application seeking for pre-emption complying with all other essential requirements stipulated under Section 96 of SAT Act, 1950. 

24. From the record, the preemptors appear to contend that the application filed by the opposite party No.23 for joining him as co-preemptor is barred by limitation. It transpires from the record that the co-preemptor filed an application on 24.061999 to join him as a preemptor, but the trial Court by order dated 24.06.1999 summarily rejected the said application with the observation that since the date of knowledge had not been mentioned in the said application the same was barred by limitation. Subsequently, the opposite party No.23 filed another application on 07.07.1999 for adding him as co-preemptor on the averment that, he is a co-sharer by inheritance in the case holding. He had been staying in Chattogram for long and he used to run a grocery shop there, but service of summon was made in his permanent address at Ekhlashpur village, Noakhali where he was not present at all at the relevant time. After coming to visit his native's home at Noakhali on 20.06.1999 he came to know about the pre-emption proceeding and alleged transfer from his brother Nurul Huda, who is opposite party No.21 in the pre-emption case and obtained the copy of pre-emption case on 22.06.1999. Earlier be filed an application for adding him as co-preemptor on 24.06.1999 within two months from the date of said knowledge. Since the date of his knowledge about the alleged transfer was not mentioned in the said application, the same was rejected on the ground of limitation. The opposite party No.23 could not know about the alleged transfer due to the fraudulent activities of the opposite parties No.1-5. No summons had been served on the opposite party No.23 at all. According to law the application for adding as co-preemptor must be filed within two months from the date of knowledge and accordingly the opposite party No.23 filed the said application within two months from the date of knowledge. The trial Court stated that the report of the process-server regarding summons was not found on the record. 

25. On scrutiny of the record, it appears that the report of the process server regarding the service of summons upon the opposite parties is available on the record which discloses that the summons of the opposite party No.23-co-preemptor has not been served upon him personally, but the same has been received by the opposite party No.21 putting his signature on behalf of the co-preemptor. Although P.W.1, Md. Yousuf admitted in his cross-examination that the co-preemptor had wife and children who live in the home they have not been sought to receive the summons on behalf of the co-preemptor. Even according to law in default of regular service, the summons would be served through affixing a copy of the summons on the outer door or some other conspicuous part of the house. But the summons on the opposite party No.23-co-preemptor has not also been served in the said manner. That apart on examination of the record it is apparent that although the opposite party No.21 and the co-preemptor both are brothers to each other, but they do not live in a joint family and after getting married they were living separately. In the premises made above, it is crystal clear that the summons on the opposite party No.23-co-preemptor has not been served as per provisions laid down in Order V of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

26. Admittedly the preemptors, co-pre-emptor, preemptees and opposite parties No.18-24 reside permanently at Ekhlashpur village in Noakhali district. O.P.W. 1 stated in his cross-examination that although co-preemptor runs his business in. Chattogram he resides permanently at Ekhlashpur village in Noakhali. O.P.W.2 stated in his cross-examination that the co-preemptor resides in Chattogram in the pursuit of his business although his family live at Ekhlashpur village in Noakhali and he comes to Ekhlashpur occasionally. 27. The co-preemptor deposed in the Court as witness No.1 on his behalf and he stated in the deposition that he is a businessperson having a grocery shop in Chattogram in the name and style 'Alamin Store' and he used to stay in Chattogram in the pursuit of his said business. In support of the aforesaid claim the co-preemptor filed Nationality Certificate dated 14.11.1994 and the Voter Identity Card (Exhibit-9). The Nationality Certificate was issued by Chattogram City Corporation while the Voter Identity Card was issued by the concerned Ward Commissioner of Chattogram City Corporation. It reveals from the Voter Identity Card that his profession was mentioned therein as business. Thus, it is evident that the co-preemptor runs business in Chattogram. Moreover, both the Exhibits-8 and 9 had been issued by the proper authority and the Nationality Certificate was issued on 14.11.1994 nearly five years before filing of the pre-emption case. Therefore, it cannot be presumed that the said Nationality Certificate was created and afterthought and had been procured fraudulently for the purpose of the pre-emption case. 

28. The co-preemptor claims that he came to know about the alleged transfer on 20.06.1999 from his brother opposite party No.21 namely Nurul Huda. The co-preemptor as witness No.1 deposed sup-porting the said claim. The witness No.2 namely Abu Taber on behalf the co-pre-emptor deposed corroborating the co-pre-emptor i.e. witness No.1 in this regard. The witness No.2 categorically stated in his deposition that the opposite party No.21 disclosed about the alleged sale to the co-preemptor in his presence on 20.06.1999 at 5:00 p.m. Therefore, the co-preemptor has been able to prove the date of knowledge about the alleged transfer. But the trial Court as well as the appellate Court below most illegally found that without examining opposite party No.21 as to the date of knowledge, the co-pre-emptor failed to prove the date of knowledge. 

29. As discussed earlier, the opposite parties No.21 and 18 are the brothers of the co-preemptor, but there is no reliable evidence on record from which it is proved that the opposite parties No.21 and 18 and the co-preemptor live in a joint family rather there is sufficient evidence in support of the facts that after marriage they are living separately. Therefore, neither the opposite party No.21 and opposite party No.18 was proved to be the agent of the co-preemptor, thus the service of summons on the opposite party No.21 on behalf of the co-preemptor has no legal effect at all. Again, having perused the alleged sale deed (Exhibit-1) it is seen that opposite party No.18 namely Md. Mostafa was named as witness No.2 in the said deed. In the light of the foregoing discussion, it is squarely proved that although the opposite parties No.18 and 21 might knew about the alleged transfer at the time of execution of the said deed (Exhibit-1) the Co-preemptor could know nothing regarding the alleged sale deed and the co-preemptor came to know about the said transfer only on 20.06.1999 from the opposite party No.21. 

30. Now it is to be looked into the laws regarding the limitation period for filing of application by a co-preemptor. Section 96(4) of SAT Act, 1950 lays down as follows: 
"(4) When an application has been made under subsection(1) any of the remaining co-sharer tenants including the transferee if one of them, and the tenants holding lands contiguous to the land transferred, may within the period referred to in sub-section (1) or within two months of the date of the service of the notice of the application under clause(b) of sub-section(3) whichever be earlier, apply to join in the said application; any co-sharer tenant or tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred who has not applied either under subsection (1) or under this sub-section, shall not have any further right to purchase under this section." 

31. The record of the case shows that the alleged sale deed was executed on 26.10.1997 and registered on 03.12.1998 while the Preemption Case was filed on 01.04.1999 and summons upon the opposite parties were served on 04.04.1999. It has already been proved that the co-pre-emptor learnt about the alleged transfer on 20.06.1999 from the opposite party No.21. The co-preemptor filed the application for adding him as co-preemptor in the Court on 24.06.1999 though the same was summarily rejected. Later on, the co-preemptor again filed the application for transposing him as co-preemptor on 07.07.1999 which was kept in the record for considering the same at the time of trial of the case. Since on examination of the record it has been unambiguously proved that the co-preemptor learnt about the alleged transfer on 22.06.1999 and he filed the application on 24.06.1999 within two months from the date of knowledge we have no hesitation to hold that the application filed by the co-preemptor for pre-emption is not barred by limitation under Section 96(4) of SAT Act, 1950. 

32. In view of the above discussion and the facts and circumstances of the case, it is our considered opinion that the co-pre-emptor is a co-sharer tenant by inheritance while the preemptors are tenants holding contiguous land and the pre-emptees are strangers. In the given premises, the co-preemptor will get priority in getting the entire case land by way of pre-emption. Therefore, the co-preemptor is entitled to get the entire case land measuring 36 decimal by way of pre-emption. 

33. In the light of the foregoing discussion and for the reasons stated above, the impugned judgment and order dated 14.01.2009 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1303 of 2003 warrants for interference by this Division and we find merit in the Civil Appeal No.71 of 2012. On the other hand, we do not find any merit in the Civil Appeal No.70 of 2012 and Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.2001 of 2021. 

34. Consequently, the Civil Appeal No.70 of 2012 and Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.2001 of 2021 are dismissed without any order as to costs. 

35. The Civil Appeal No.71 of 2012 is allowed. 

36. The appellant Abul Kashem is allowed to get the entire case land by way of pre-emption. The preemptors are entitled to get back the money already deposited by him in the Court while the co-preemptor shall deposit the total amount of money required for the pre-emption of the case land if he has not already: deposited the same. 

37. The impugned judgment and order dated 14.01.2009 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.1303 of 2003, so far as it relates to the grant of half of the case land for pre-emption in favour of the pre-emptors, is set aside. 

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.160 of 2024
lawyer:
Mr. A. M Amin Uddin, Senior Advocate with Mr Mushtaque Ahmad Chowdhury, Advocate and Mr Shah Mohammad Ezaz Rahman, Advocate instructed by Mr. Mohammad Ali Azam, Advocate-on-Record. -------- For the Petitioner

parties:
Sadia Nowsin Sikder. -------- Petitioner.
Vs.
Md. Nehal Sikder and others. -------- Respondents.
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 28.11.2023 passed by the High Court Division in First Miscellaneous Appeal No.316 of 2023 connected with Civil Rule No.782 (FM) of 2023)
full_judgment:
Borhanuddin J. This civil petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 28.11.2023 passed by the High Court Division in First Miscellaneous Appeal No.316 of 2023 connected with Civil Rule No.782 of 2023 disposing of the appeal and the connected Rule with a direction upon the trial Court to dispose o the Title Suit No.78 of 2023 within a period of 6(six) months from the date of receipt of the copy of the judgment and order with a further direction upon the parties to maintain status quo in respect of schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha' properties as passed by the High Court Division vide order dated 29.08.2023 in the connected civil Rule. 

2. Background of the case is that the respondent no.1 herein as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No.78 of 2023 in the Court-of learned Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka for declaration and partition, contending interalia, that Mrs. Layla Sikdcr, Mother of the plaintiff and defendant no.1, obtained title of the suit schedule 'Ka' land vide registered Sale Deed No.9195 dated 20.12.1972 from the original lessee of the land Wakil Ahmed; City Jorip Khatian No.1234 of the 'Ka' schedule land was correctly published in her name; Plaintiff and defendant no.1 used to stay in the land with their mother; Said land was rented to the Iranian Culture Centre since 01.11.2013 and the centre was there till 2021; Mother of the plaintiff used to reside there with the defendant no.1; Mother of the plaintiff had to undergone glaucoma operation and upon two successive operation in 2010 and 2011, she lost her eye sight; Between 2008-2016 the plaintiff has visited Singapore on numerous occasions for treatment of heart disease; Taking advantage of the ill health of their mother as well as plaintiff, the defendant no.1 managed to procure the deed in question relating to schedule 'Ka' land by practicing fraud; Similarly schedule 'Kha' apartment was also obtained by practicing fraud. After demise of the plaintiffs mother all on a sudden the building of the-schedule 'Ka' land was demolished. 

3. Then the plaintiff requested the defendant no.1 for partition of the ejmali properties but the defendant no.1 lastly refused to enter into a partition on 03.02.2023 which constrained the plaintiff to file instant suit for declaration of title and partition of the schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha' properties claiming the same as ejmali property and schedule 'Gha' and 'Uma' documents are not binding upon him; Lateron the Trial Court allowed an application for amendment of the plaint and accordingly added schedule 'Kha-1' to 'Kha-5' properties in the sched-ule of the plaint alongwith schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha' properties; Upon filing of the suit, the plaintiff-petitioner filed an application for temporary injunction under. Order 39 Rule 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure; The Trial Court passed an ad-interim order of statu-quo in respect of possession, position and transferring schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha' properties vide order dated 12.04.2023; On 07.05.2023, the defendant entered her appearance and on 28.05.2023 filed a written objection against the application for temporary injunction; On 09.08.2023, a supplementary was also filed by the defendant no.1 to the said written objection; On 28.05.2023, the defendant no.1 filed an application under Rule 5A(3) of Order 39 of the Code of Civil Procedure for vacating the ad-interim order of status-quo which was kept in the record by the Trial Court with an observation that the said order of status-quo has ceased upon filing of the written objection by the defendant-opposite party; On 08.06.2023, the plaintiff filed an application for addition of party stating that proforma respondent no.6, Shanta Holding Limited, as developer hanged a signboard in the schedule 'Ka' property and started construction therein and as such the said developer company is required to be added as defendant no.5 in the suit and accordingly Shanta Holding Limited was added as defendant no.5; The plaintiff on 25.06.2023 filed an application for amendment of the plaint inserting certain new schedules in the plaint describing certain fraudulent activities. The plaintiff also filed an application for amending the application for temporary injunction; Upon hearing, the Trial Court allowed the application for amendment of the plaint and kept the application for amendment of the application for temporary injunction till hearing of the original application; On 22.08.2023, the plaintiff filed an application under Order 39 Rule 7 for local inspection with an application praying not to pass any order till disposal of the application for local inspection; The learned Joint District Judge vide its Order No.14 dated 22.08.2023 disallowed the application dated 25.06.2023 for amendment of the application for temporary injunction and thereby reject the-application for temporary injunction on contest and fixed another date for hearing of the application for local inspection; Challenging the Order No.14 dated 22.08.2023 passed by the learned Join District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka, the plaintiff a appellant preferred F.M.A.T. No.361 of 2023 before the High Court Division and also filed an application for temporary injunction on 28.08.2023 which is numbered as Civil Rule No.782(FM) of 2023; On 29.08.2023, the High Court Division passed an order of status-quo upon the parties in respect of suit schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha' properties; Having came to know about the order of status-quo passed by the High Court Division, the present petitioner alongwith the pro-forma respondent no.6 entered their appearances in the aforesaid civil Rule and filed an application in the First Miscellaneous Appeal No.316 of 2023 seeking permission to continue construction in the suit scheduled 'Ka' land. 

4. After hearing the parties, a Division Bench of the High Court Division dis-posed of the FMA No.316 of 2023 along-with the connected Rule by the impugned judgment and order dated 28.11.2023. 

5. Challenging the impugned judgment and order the defendant-respondent no.1 as petitioner preferred instant civil petition for leave to appeal invoking Article 103(3) of the Constitution. 

6. Mr. A. M. Amin Uddin, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that the High Court Division erroneously passed the impugned judgment and order without considering that admittedly the, schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha' properties belonged to Mrs. Layla Sikder, mother of the present petitioner and respondent no.1, as a lessee under the Ministry of Housing and Public Works and the RAJUK respectively and said Mrs. Layla Sikder by observing all legal formalities lawfully transferred the leasehold title and ownership of the schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha' properties to her daughter Sadia Nowsin Sikder, the present petitioner, by dint of two separate registered heba deeds and the present petitioner after obtaining necessary permission mutated her name and paying rents and taxes regularly having transferrable right, title and possession over the suit land without any hindrance from anyone else and as such the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set-aside. He also submits that the High Court Division failed to take into consideration that the pro-forma respondent no.6, Shanta Holding Limited, complying all the terms and conditions entered into the registered deed of agreement with the present petitioner for construction of multi-storied building in the schedule 'Ka' property and also obtained an irrevocable general power of attorney from the present petitioner and thereafter also obtained approval from RAJUK for construction and as such the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set-aside. He next submits that the High Court Division failed to take into consideration that the respondent no.1 has no legal right to claim the schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha' properties since the same are not ejmali properties rather those are the leasehold properties belonging to the present lessee who obtained the ownership and title by dint of two separate registered heba deeds after completing all legal formalities and the respondent no.1 miserably failed to provide any material statement or allegation in the plaint that the present petitioner obtained the lease-hold title and possession by practicing fraud as such the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set-aside. 

7. On the other hand. Mr. Sk. Md. Morshed, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent no.1 supports the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division. 

8. Heard the learned Advocates for the parties and perused the papers/documents contained in the paper book. 

9. It appears that the respondent no.1 here-in as plaintiff filed the suit for declaration of title and partition claiming that suit schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha' properties are ejmali properties and the suit schedule 'Ga-Uma' documents are not binding upon the plaintiff. Admittedly, the suit schedule 'Ka' property belonged to Mrs. Layla Sikder, mother of the petitioner and respondent no.1, who obtained title of the land vide registered sale deed from the original lessee. Plaintiff filed the suit claiming that the present petitioner, defendant no.1 of the suit, managed to procure the heba deed relating schedule 'Ka' land by practicing fraud and similarly obtained schedule 'Kha' apartment by practicing fraud. The respondent no.1-plaintiff filed an application in the suit under Order 39 Rule 1 and 2 read with Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for temporary injunction barring defendant no.1 of the suit from constructing any structure or changing nature and character of the 'Ka' schedule land or transfer suit schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha' land till disposal of the suit. The petitioner-defendant no.1 filed written objection denying material averments made in the application and prayed for rejecting the same. The Trial Court upon contested hearing rejected the application for temporary injunction holding that since soon after filing of the suit the defendant-opposite party no.1 as plaintiff filed Title Suit No.503 of 2023 impleading the plaintiff-appellant as defendant therein for partition and the subject matter and remedy sought in the suit and that of the subject matter and remedy sought in the application for temporary injunction are same, so the plaintiff-appellant can contest the said suit by filing a written statement narrating his case and all his grievances can be addressed in the said suit. So, there is no reason to get any ad-interim order in the suit vis-a-vis the defendant-opposite party no.1 has already appointed a developer, defendant no.5, to build apartments on the land of 'Ka' schedule. Thus, the balance of convenience and inconvenience stands not infavour of the plaintiff rather for the dependants. 

10. By now it is settled that in a suit for partition the court always follows a principle not to pass any restraining order to any co-sharer until and unless the parties to such suit can satisfy the court that he/she has been in exclusive possession over specific portion of an undivided property. 

11. It is also well settled that in a suit for partition every co-sharer of an undivided property is entitle to enjoy every inch of land until and unless the same is partitioned through metes and bounds by a competent court except any co-sharer is found to enjoy in specific portion of the undivided land, then an injunction can be granted thereon and since 'Ka' schedule property is now belong to the defendant no.1 and the deed of gift has not yet been declared illegal, so the defendant no.1 has rightly furnished an agreement with the defendant no.5 for constructing apartments thereon. 

12. It also appears that the petitioner is ready to give undertaken to the effect that if the plaintiff ultimately gets decree in the suit then he would surrender two-third of the apartments infavur of the plaintiff, even though the defendant no.5 be allowed to continue construction work on 'Ka' schedule land by disposing of the appeal and Rule. It also appears that apart from 'Ka' and 'Kha' schedule land, there have been other properties belonged to the mother of the plaintiff and defendant no. l. 

13. Thus, it appears that the High Court Division without considering the facts and circumstances of the case erroneously directed the parties to maintain status-quo in respect of suit schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha' properties vide judgment and order dated 28.11.2023, which calls interference by this Division. 

14. The impugned judgment and order dated 28.11.2.023 passed by the High Court Division is hereby set-aside. 

15. The order of status-quo passed by the High Court Division is hereby vacated. The Trial Court is directed to conclude the trial within 06(six) months from the date of receipt a copy of this judgment and order. 50% land ownership share of the suit schedule land shall not be transferred pursuant to undertaken furnished by the petitioner. 

16. Accordingly, the civil petition for leave to appeal is disposed of with the above observation and direction. 

17. Communicate a copy of this judgment and order to the Court concerned. 

18. However, no order as to costs. 

End.

lawyer:

parties:
Free School Street Property Limited ------ Petitioner
vs
Chairman, Court of Settlement and anr ------- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md. Iqbal Kabir, J : This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the Respondents to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 29-5-2006 vide Annexure-C passed by the Court of Settlement in Case No. 336 of 1992 in respect of holding No. 969/1077 Bagmoniran, 3 Surson Road, Chittagong published in the 'Ka' list of the abandoned buildings should not be declared to have been made illegally and without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. Relevant facts necessary for the disposal of the Rule Nisi, in brief, are that petitioner company purchased a total of 5 acres of land in the year 1951 in which the disputed land measuring 0.018 acres was mentioned as Schedule-B to the writ petition. The alleged property belonged to Bhuban Mohan Mukhopadhay Mukherjee and Srimati Nani Bala Devi which was recorded in the name of Bhuban Mohan under PS Khatian. Thereafter, it was recorded in the name of MM Ispahani, under the BS Khatian, being owner the petitioner company sold many portions thereof. The petitioner company constructed a two-storied building on a part of the said land and office bearers of the petitioner company lived therein. However, the petitioner company was in exclusive possession of the disputed 0.018 acres of land till the Liberation in 1971 and after the Liberation War, the said building was taken over by the Government authorities evicting the company's occupants. But the rest of the land has been under the possession of the petitioner company. After the independence, the petitioner company by several applications requested the authorities to release the property, but the authority did not take any effective steps to release the same. Subsequently, the said property was included in the 'Ka' list of the abandoned buildings published on 23-9-1986 and, therefore, the petitioner company preferred a case before the learned Court of Settlement under section 7(1) of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 praying for the release of the said property in question. Thereafter, the said case was numbered as Case No. 336 of 1992, which was tried by the 2nd Court of Settlement, Dhaka. Afterward, on contest learned Court of Settlement by its judgment and order rejected the same. 

3. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order, the petitioner filed this application for judicial review before this Court and obtained the Rule Nisi. 

4. Mr. Tirtha Salil Pal, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner having taken us through the writ petition and other documents filed by the parties submits that the petitioner company purchased the concerned property directly in its name as the 'Purchaser' vide registered Deed of Sale No. 640 dated 7-2-1951. He claims that the petitioner company was incorporated in the year 1920 in the Province of Bengal therefore, the petitioner's property cannot be considered to be a subject of abandoned property. 

5. He submits that all the shareholders and Directors of the petitioner company belonged to the Ispahani family which was renowned as a business family and all their business concerns were popularly known as MM Ispahani. According to him BS survey clearly states the property was recorded and mutated in the name of MM Ispahai company. 

6. He submits that after the liberation war by a Gazette Notification dated 27-6-1974 all buildings and properties of Ispahani Group of Industries Limited and MM Ispahani Limited were released. As such no criteria for considering the property of Ispahani family/ Ispahani company as abandoned property can be satisfied and sustained. Mr. Tirtha Salil Pal argued that property of the petitioner company or the property of the Ispahani family cannot be treated as abandoned property. In his submission, he argued in response to the application dated 20-4-1983 Deputy Commissioner vide it Memo dated 17-12-1985 recommended to release the property in question in favour of the petitioner and in that respect he writes a letter to the Divisional Commissioner Sr the Chairman of the Management Board of Abandoned Property, Chittagong. 

7. He submits that the learned Court took the decision based on the title of the concerned property mentioning that Nani Bala Devi executed the said deed of sale along with her husband Bhuban Mohan but the name of Nani Bala was not included in the PS Khatian. He argued that the Court below wrongly took such an issue and decided the matter. According to him, Settlement Court had no authority to consider such issues for deciding a case of abandoned property which is absolutely beyond the jurisdiction. 

8. He claims that the Government made an oral submission against the petitioner concerning the absence in the country during the Liberation War and acted against the interest of the country. Those submissions were without supporting documents or evidence is baseless and cannot be a deciding factor in a judgment that is eventually detrimental to the rights of the petitioner property as conferred by Article 42 of the Constitution. Hence, the impugned judgment is erroneous and, therefore, liable to be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 

9. The Rule Nisi having been served upon the Respondents, on behalf of Respondent No. 2, Mr. Sukumar Biswas, learned Advocate entered an appearance and contested the same. 

10. Respondent No. 2 by filing an affidavit-in-opposition denied material assertions made in the petition, however, with regards to the statement made in the petition, Respondent states that petitioner did not file any application as prescribed in Article 15(1) and (2) of the PO 16 of 1972 within the stipulated time for releasing the property, but claimant asserted in the application filed under section 7(1) of the Ordinance LIV of 1985 read with section 8(1)(d) that the Government had taken possession of the property after liberation. The case property had ceased to occupy and uncared during the liberation war, no one supervise and or manage the property in person at the material point of time i.e., on 28-2-1972, and thus, the property itself had assumed the abandoned character under Article 2(1) of the PO 16 of 1972 and accordingly, vest upon the Government. 

11. Further states the Court of settlement by its judgment and order rightly rejected the claimant's case holding that the party seeking relief before the Court did not appear with a clean hand. In the instant case, the documents furnished do not vindicate that the petitioner's company is a sister concern of Messer's MM Ispahani Ltd., admittedly the petitioner was not in the country during the war of liberation. Apart from that, the papers concerning payments of revenue and holding tax by the petitioner company seem to have been obtained recently to establish possession over the case land. It is clear from the findings of the Court of settlement that the claimant has failed to prove his case. The claimant was not in a position to take care, manage and control the case property in person thus, the case property itself had assumed the character of abandonment and vested with the Government under Article 2(1) and 4 of PO 16 of 1972, thereafter, the Government published the same in the official Gazette dated 23-9-1986 as 'Ka' list of the Abandoned buildings which is the conclusive proof of the fact and possessing the property through its tenants since 1972. 

12. He submits that according to the provision of section 5(1)(b) of the Ordinance LIV of 1985, the inclusion of the property in the list so published is called conclusive evidence of fact under section 5(2) of the Ordinance and the same has been vested upon Government with effect from 28-2-1972. The petitioner has failed to rebut the legal presumption of law and facts by producing positive evidence regarding whereabouts and possession by paying utility bills from 26-3-1971 to 28-2-1972 and onwards. Moreover, Paragraphs "e, g, and h" of the application clearly state that the property was in possession till its possession was taken over by the Government therefore, the claimant cannot travel beyond the plaint. Moreover, residential property of the petitioner company itself had assumed the character of Abandoned Property as defined in Article 2(1) of the PO 16 of 1972. 

13. He submits that onus squarely lies upon the claimant only to prove that the property is not an abandoned property, on the other hand, the Government has no obligation either to deny the facts as alleged by the claimant or to disclose the basis of treating the property as abandoned property merely because the same is disputed by the claimant, the claimant having hopelessly failed to rebut the presumption of the conclusiveness of the Gazette by disclosing the four characters of person concurrently at the material time, so any single failure on the part of the petitioner is fully and wholly stunning, therefore, the judgment and order passed by the Court of Settlement should be sustained in law. 

14. He submits that writ of certiorari is maintainable only if it can be shown that the tribunal erroneously held that the property was illegally declared as abandoned property without admitting legal evidence or it has misconstrued the law. He argued that the claimant had failed to produce all the positive documents for excluding his property from the 'Ka' list of an abandoned building, tribunal examined all the documents about the claim of the claimant and correctly assessed and rejected the claim rightly as a final Court of facts. 

15. This Court perused the application, affidavit-in-opposition, the impugned judgment, other documents, considered the facts and submissions of the contending parties. 

16. In this case, petitioner claims that the petitioner's property cannot be considered to be a subject of abandoned property. The property would fall under Ispahani group and would be included in the gazette notification by which all buildings and properties of Ispahani Group of Industries Limited and MM Ispahani Limited were released. 

17. It is noted in this case, petitioner did not file any application as prescribed in law within the stipulated time for releasing the property. Therefore, the claimant was required to file a petition before the Settlement Court the petitioner filed such an application under law. From the application, it appears the claimant admitted the owner of the property did not have possession during the period of the liberation war. Thus, the property was rightly enlisted as abandoned property by operation of law. In this case, Mr. Biswas, learned Advocate relied upon the decision namely Secretary, Ministry of Works and others vs Rowshan Ara Begum and another, reported in 57 DLR (AD) 167, Bangladesh vs Md. Jalil and others reported in 48 DLR (AD) 10 and argued that the onus, therefore, is squarely on the claimant of the building to prove that the building is not an abandoned property. The Government has no obligation either to deny the facts alleged by the claimant or to disclose the basis of treating the property as abandoned property merely because the same is disputed by the claimants. 

18. In course of the hearing, this Court was directed to produce the original file or record before this Court and as per the direction, Mr. Sukumar Biswas learned Advocate produced the relevant record in respect of the settlement case record before this Court. 

19. From the record and the submission of the Respondent it also transpires to us that the petitioner did not produce any positive document or evidence to rebut the legal presumption of law and facts by adducing witness regarding possession receipts showing payment of utility bills, municipal Tax receipt since 26-3-71 and onwards. Though, the petitioner by filing supplementary affidavit produces few documents to this Court which was not before the Court of Settlement. This Court is not a Court of appeal, thus, this Court has no authority to assess those documents which were not before the Court of Settlement. 

20. Further, it is noted that considering the relevant papers, the owner of the alleged abandoned property was Free School Street Property Limited, and it was not a sister concern of MM Ispahani or not managing as an agent of MM Ispahani. The Court of Settlement found on consideration of the materials on record that the petitioner could not provide any document about managing the claimed property through the agent and could not also produce other documents from 1972 to 2004, the document which has produced all are after 2005. Thus, the submission of the petitioner is not sustainable in law and the facts. In this instant case, the tribunal examined all the documents concerning the claim of the claimant and acted rightly as a final Court of fact. 

21. It is further noted that this Court while examining the correctness of the judgment of the subordinate tribunal does not act as the Court of appeal and on this account an authority wherein it was held in the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Md. Jalil and others reported in 48 DLR (AD) 10 "The High Court Division was not a Court of appeal required to determine facts on its own. It could interfere with the findings of a tribunal of fact under its extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 102 only if it could be shown that the tribunal had acted without jurisdiction or made any finding upon no evidence or not considering in material evidence/facts causing prejudice to the complaining party or that it had acted mala fide or in violation of any principle of natural justice. In the absence of any of these conditions the interference by the High Court Division will itself be an act of without jurisdiction". Further, in the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Ashraf Ali and another, reported in 49 DLR (AD) 161 it has been held that the High Court Division while exercising its power under certiorari in connection with the judgment of an 'inferior tribunal' is not within its jurisdiction if it acts in a manner or that considering the materials record in the manner "in which a Court of appeal dispossess of an appeal". 

22. Mr. Tirtha Salil Pal, learned Advocate for the petitioner by showing Annexure-B (1) to the writ petition claims that the Government released few concerns with immediate effect including Buildings and Properties of MM Ispahani Ltd. 

23. It is at this juncture that this Court has taken into consideration Mr. AAG's submission that the following concerns of the Ispahani Group of Industries and Companies which were taken over under the Bangladesh (Taking over of Control and Management of Industrial Commercial Concerns) Order-1972 on the plea that the "owner and management have left Bangladesh and not available." is and the subject matter of this petitioner's claim relates to Industrial Building and Properties of MM Ispahani Ltd. which had been taken over by the Government, the Ministry of Industries, Industries Division as abandoned industry according to section 3 of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Industries) Rules-1972, whereas the petitioner's property is the residential property measuring area 0.018 acres in which the residential building is situated and nothing abandoned by the management of Free School Street Property Ltd, hence it had assumed the character of abandoned property within the mischief of Article 2(1) of the PO 16 of 1972, thus, the above mentioned gazette does not attract the property of the petitioner company i.e., the Free School Street Property Ltd. The Government took over the possession of the said property as abandoned and published the Gazette on 23rd September 1986 in 'Ka' list as Serial No. 252 which is a conclusive proof of facts as well as law. 

24. It is noted that by the notification dated 27-6-1974 property of the MM Ispahai was released, but, petitioner or MM Ispahini did not file any representation and sought to release the alleged property petitioner brought our notice that a representation dated 20-4-1983 (Annexure-F to the supplementary affidavit filed by the petitioner) was filed to release the property as all other properties have already been released. Further, it was claimed by the Respondent that the property of Free School Street Property Ltd. is not a commercial or Industrial Property rather it is a residential building situated in urban areas and falls within the ambit of Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Building in Urban Areas) Rules-1972. According to Mr. Biswas, the disputed property was taken over by the authority under the Ministry of Works presently Ministry of Housing and Public works following Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Taking over Possession) Rules-1972, and finally gazette has been published. 

25. However, it is noted that the petitioner relying upon a document (as Annexure-G) claims that authority recommended releasing of the property by notification dated 27-6-1974 and released the Ispahani's property. On our scrutiny, it is evident that alleged notification clearly states to release those concerns of Ispahani Group of Industries Companies which were taken over, vide notification Nos. 4A-27/72/27/148(6) dated 30-3-1972 and 3A-XV-7/73/Pt/523, dated 27-9-1993 and 19-10-1973 only. It is evident from the recommendation letter issued by Deputy Commissioner (Annexure-G) that the alleged property was abandoned on 24-8-73, not on the date as mentioned in the gazette. On a combined reading of those two documents, it reveals that only those property have been released which were declaied abandoned and taken over vide notification Nos. 4A-27/72/27/148(6) dated 30-3-1972 and 3A-XV-7/73/Pt/523, dated 27-9-1993 and 19-10-1973 and nothing other than those properties were even released as mentioned in the Gazette. In the notification dated 27-6-1974 this particular property was not included as it was not declared abandoned on such date that has mentioned in the gazette therefore, no scope or question does not arise to release the property in question. 

26. Further, it is pertinent to note that the issue of title of the property in question has been brought by the petitioner before the Settlement Court. Therefore, based on the documents produced by the petitioner, Court below discussed the issue in a limited manner which was required, but Court did not exceed its limit. 

27. Mr. Tirtha Salil Pal in support of his submission cited several decisions such as Mls Gannysons Ltd. vs Sonali Bank & others, reported in 37 DLR (AD) 42; Hamidul Huq Chowdhury & others vs Bangladesh & others, reported in 33 DLR 381; Mls. Khan Brothers Ltd. vs Bangladesh & others, reported in 27 DLR 423, S. Speed Bird Navigation Co. & others vs Bangladesh & others, reported in 27 DLR 170; and Mls. Helal Jute Press Ltd. vs Bangladesh & others, reported in 27 DLR 551. However, it appears that the facts and circumstances of the present case are different from those of the reported cases cited by the learned Advocate for the Respondent. So those cases have no manner of application to the present case, therefore, we are unable to accept any of the contentions as raised by the Advocate for the petitioner. 

28. From the above discussion, upon meticulous perusal of the papers and documents appended to this application it is clear that the owner did not have any possession over the property. The whereabouts of the petitioner was not known at the relevant point of time rather the papers appended to this application conclusively show that the owner was not in actual physical possession and no document shows it was managed by an agent and a sister concern of the Ispahani group. Therefore, it does not fall within the ambit of the gazette as alleged by the petitioner. 

29. In the light of the discussion as made above, this Court did not find any substance and force in the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the petitioner. On contrary, we find substance in the submission made by the learned Advocate for the Respondent No. 2. 

30. For the reason discussed hereinbefore, we are of the view that there is no merit in the Rule Nisi. 

31. Accordingly, the Rule is discharged. 

32. Send down the lower court record. 

33. No Order as to Costs. 

Communicate the Order. 

End.
