Accordingly, the Delimitation Officer by his memo No. stha:nita: /lal/98/684 dated 5-6-98 served the notices upon the objections about the said hearing before the Joint Secretary in the Ministry on 7-6-98. We find from record that on 7-6-98 the Delimitation Officer and all the 12 objectors were present for hearing before the Joint Secretary, Prescribed Authority and they were given proper opportunity of hearing. It appears from page 120 of the office file that the prescribed authority after hearing the objectors and considering their case by order dated 7-6-98 gave its decision for some amendments and alterations in the preliminary list of wards and directed the Delimitation Officer to publish the final list of wards in the following terms:

“৭-৬-৯৮ ইং অদ্য লালমোহন পৌরসভার ওয়ার্ড বিভক্তি বিষয়ে শুনানীর জন্য ধার্য আছে ডিলিমিটেপশন অফিসার উপস্থিত আপত্তি কারীগণের ১২ জন হাজির। উভয় পক্ষের বক্তব্য শুনা হল। সংশ্লিষ্ট কাগজপত্র পর্যালোচনা করা হল। ভৌগলিক প্রশাসনিক ও জনসংখ্যার সমতা বিধান পূর্বক ওয়ার্ড বিভক্তির লক্ষ্যে ডিলিমিটেশন অফিসার কর্তৃক প্রকাশিত লালমোহন পৌরসভার প্রিলিমিনারী ওয়ার্ড তালিকায় নিম্নোক্ত অংশ প্রস্তাবিত ৬নং ওয়ার্ড হতে বিয়োজন করে ৪নং ওয়ার্ড-এ সংযোজনের সিদ্ধান্ত হল। করিম রোডের পার্শ্বে অবস্থিত পাটোয়ারী বাড়ী ও কাঞ্চনদের বাড়ীর সামানে দিয়া সোজা পশ্চিম দিকে দত্তপাড়া এবং পাটোয়ার�� বাড়ীর মাঝখান দিয়ে আনিসুল হকের সারের দোকানের সামনের আর এন্ড এইচ রোড থেকে দক্ষিণে এগিয়ে পশ্চিম দিকে লঞ্চ ঘাট রাস্তা ধরে লালমোহনের খাল পর্যন্ত অংশ।

উপরোক্ত রূপে প্রিলিমিনারী ওয়ার্ড তালিকা সংশোধন পূর্বক চুড়ান্ত তালিকা প্রকাশ করে উহার সত্যায়িত কপি আগামী ১০-৬-৯৮ ইং তারিখের মধ্যে অত্র মন্ত্রনালয়ে পৌছানোর জন্য ডিলিমিটেশন অফিসার কে বলা হয়।”

The aforesaid order of the prescribed authority was communicated to the Delimitation Officer by Memo No. poura-2/ward-6/98/ 816 dated 7-6-98. We have already noticed from the office record that the petitioner Md Abdul Mannan did not file any objection before the respondent No. 2 after publication of the preliminary list dated 17-5-98 and that those 12 persons who filed objections were notified to appear before the prescribed authority for hearing. We find from the official record that in compliance with the direction of the authority dated 7-6-98 the Delimitation Officer, under section 21(4) and 21(5) of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 made necessary amendments, corrections, alterations and modifications of the preliminary list dated 17-5-98 and published the final list of wards specifying the areas included in such wards under memo No. thana/ni: A/Lal/98/745 (500) dated 9-6-98. In the course of hearing the learned Deputy Attorney General referred to us a copy of memo No. 91 dated 7-6-99 (Annexure-1 to the supplementary affidavit) issued by the Thana Statistical Officer Lalmohan, Bhola to the Delimitation Officer, Thana Nirbahi Officer, stating that there is no scope for supplying upto-date information regarding ward wise distribution of population of the newly created 9 wards because there was no census after 1991 and no survey was conducted thereafter. Section 21 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 is as follows:

"21 Delimitation of Wards (1) The wards shall be delimited having regard to territorial unity and, so far as practicable, to distribution of population (save with a variation of not more than ten percent) and administrative convenience.

(2) A delimitation officer may, for the purpose of delimiting the wards, make such enquiries and examine such records as he may deem necessary and consider such representations as may be received by him, and shall publish at his office and at the office of the Pourashava and at such other place or places as he considers necessary a preliminary list of wards specifying the areas proposed to be included in each ward together with a notice inviting objections or suggestions within fifteen days from the date of publication of the notice.

(3) The objection or suggestion, if any, received under sub-section (2) shall be forwarded to the prescribed authority who, after making such enquiries as he considers necessary, shall give its decision within a period not exceeding fifteen days from the date of receipt of the objections or suggestions from the delimitation officer.

(4) The delimitation officer shall make such amendments, alterations or modifications in the preliminary list published under sub-section (2) as may be required by any decision on any objection or suggestion given by the prescribed authority under sub-section (3) and may also make such other amendments, alterations or modifications in the said list as may be necessary for correcting any error or omission.

(5) After making amendments, alterations or modifications, if any, under sub-section (4), the delimitation officer shall publish at his office and at the office of the Pourashava and at such other place or place as he considers necessary the final list of wards, specifying the areas included in such ward and shall forward attested copies thereof to the prescribed authority who shall publish the list of wards in the official Gazette".

<u>19. Sub-section 1 of section 21 provides that so far as practicable the distribution of population save with a variation of not more than 10% should be taken into consideration. Since there was no means of ascertaining up to date correct number of the ward wise distribution of population of newly created 9 wards, the Delimitation Officer, in the facts and circumstance of the case having complied with the provisions of law by obtaining necessary information so far as practicable from the Thana Statistical Officer as we have noticed from the official record and as evident from the memo No. 91 dated 7-6-99 (Annexure-1 to the supplementary affidavit) delimited 3 wards into 9 wards. We are of the view that the correct number of ward wise distribution of population of the newly created 9 wards could not be ascertained by the Delimitation Officer, in the prevailing circumstances and he was competent enough under the law to effect the delimitation of 9 wards on the basis of necessary information available regarding territorial unity and so far as practicable distribution of population save with a variation of not more than ten percent and administrative convenience. We are of the view that the distribution of population in 9 wards with a variation of not more than ten percent being a disputed question of fact cannot be decided in writ jurisdiction. We do not find any substance in the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the petitioner. It has already been noticed from the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the respondents and the official record that the final list of wards was published in the official Gazette on 2-7-1998 in compliance with the requirements of law by the prescribed authority. For the aforesaid reasons we do not find any merit in the Rule issued in Writ Petition No. 1787 of 1998.</u>

20. In Writ Petition No. 2259 of 1998 we have found from Annexure-B that the respondent No. 4, Delimitation Officer, issued the preliminary notification vide memo No. 346(7) dated 6-5-1998 inviting objections and suggestions from the people of the Pourashava area and copies of the said notice were circulated in conspicuous parts of different areas of the Pourashava and sent to the local Member of the Parliament, the Deputy Commissioner Noakhali, Assistant Commissioner (Land), Sub-Registrar. Choumuhani and the notice board of the Thana Nirbahi Officer and the Chairman of Choumuhani Pourashava who received the same on 14-5-98 It appears from Annexure-E that considering the objections and suggestions the Delimitation Officer modified the said notice and issued the preliminary list of wards vide Memo No. 376 (6) dated 21-5-98 and forwarded the same to the prescribed authority in the Ministry, the Deputy Commissioner and other functionaries of the Government. We have also found from Annexure-G that respondent No. 2, Deputy Secretary (Poura) issued notice of objection hearing vide Memo No. 721 (5) dated 27-5-98 asking the objectors to be present for objection hearing before Md Moksumul Hoque, Joint Secretary of the said Ministry on 31-5-98 at 9-30 AM. We find substance in the submission of the learned Deputy Attorney General that during the time of objection hearing on 31-5-98 at 9-00 AM before the prescribed authority, the Delimitation Officer appeared personally with all the written objections filed by the people of the Pourashava area against preliminary list of wards and all objectors were present and they were given opportunity of hearing as per section 21(3) and the prescribed authority gave its decision for necessary amendments, alterations and modifications of the preliminary list of wards. We have found that the Delimitation Officer as per decisions of the Prescribed Authority under section 21(4) and 21(5) of the said Ordinance made required amendments, alterations and modifications of all newly created wards except wards Nos. 5, 6 and 9 of the preliminary list of wards and published the final list of wards a/ evident from Memo No. 432 dated 6-6- 98 and forwarded the same to the prescribed authority under memo No. 433 dated 6-6-1998 (Annexure-1). It appears from Annexure-L that the prescribed authority by Memo No. Poura-2/Ward-6/, 98/817 dated 8-6-1998 published the final list of wards in the official Gazette on 2-7-1998. We have noticed that in making delimitation of 3 wards into 9 wards the Delimitation Officer has taken into consideration of the territorial unity and so far as practicable distribution of population save with a variation of not more than ten percent and administrative convenience. We have also noticed that territorial boundaries of previous wards were given preference and taken into consideration as demarcation line and territorial unity of Choumuhani Bazar was presented and Golabaria are previously included in the Bazar was also subsequently kept in the same ward and some of the natural boundaries like internal canal and roads under R&H Department, important roads of Pourashava and mouza boundary were taken into consideration in making the delimitation process in accordance with section 21(1) of the said Ordinance. We do not find any substance in the contentions of Mr Moudud Ahmed that the distribution of population on the basis of 1991 census as appeared in Annexure-I at page 64 of the writ petition is wrong and as per Memo No. 424 dated 14-6-99 (Annexure-P) said to have been issued by the Choumuhani Pourashava variation of the population is more than 10% in the respective wards. We have already judicially noticed that no census was held after 1991 and in Writ Petition No. 1787 of 1998 the Thana Statistical Officer, Lalmohan, District Bhola vide Memo No. 91 dated 7-6-99 (Annexure-1 to supplementary affidavit) informed the Delimitation Officer, Lalmohan that since 1991 no census has been held and it was not possible for the Statistical Bureau to supply present number of ward wise distribution of population of the newly created 9 wards of Lalmohan Pourashava. As we have noticed that there is no scope for ascertaining the present number of distribution of population of the newly created 9 wards of Choumuhani Pourashava, the respondent No. 4, Delimitation Officer, having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case, has rightly taken the population of 1991 census as the basis so far as practicable for distribution of population save with a variation of not more than 10% in the said 9 wards. We find that there is substance in the submissions of the learned Deputy Attorney General that Annexure-P said to have been issued by Choumuhani Pourashava has no relevance in the disposal of the present Rule because no census having been held since 1991 there is no scope for ascertaining the present number of ward wise distribution of population in the newly created 9 wards. This also finds support from Annexure-O (1) to the affidavit-in-reply filed by the petitioner where the Thana. Statistical Officer, Begumganj vide memo dated 10-5-99 stated that.

21. From a clear reading of the provisions of the sub-section (1) of section 21 of the said Ordinance we are of the view that these are directory and not mandatory. From the very wordings of sub-section 1 of section 21 so far as practicable to distribution of population save with a variation of not more than 10% we find that these words 'save with a variation of not more than 10% are prefixed by the words so far as practicable' which means that variation of not more than 10% depends on the practical circumstance of a particular case and the Delimitation Officer having had information regarding population so far as available, is required to make distribution of population in 9 wards in the light of the practical circumstance, i.e. given facts and figures. So, we are of the view that the provision of section 21 is directory and not mandatory. As regards territorial unity and administrative convenience the petitioners have failed to prove any violation of the provisions of section 21 of the said Ordinance. So, we do not find any illegality in the impugned notification of final list of wards as regards, territorial unity and administrative convenience. We find substance in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the respondents that the petitioner Nos. 1 and 6 being the Commissioner and the Chairman respectively of the Choumuhani Pourashava, after the expiry of the term of office filed the writ petition on the alleged ground of violation of section 21 to delay the election of the Pourashava and to continue in the said office and obtained a Rule which is not sustainable in law. In the facts and circumstances stated above and for the aforesaid reasons, we find that there is no merit in the Rule in the Writ Petition No. 2259 of 1998.

“নতুন ওয়ার্ড হওয়ার পর ইহার কোন শুমারী না হওয়ার কারণে বর্তমান জনসংখ্যা নতুন ওয়ার্ডভিত্তিক সরবরাহ করা সম্ভব হয় নাই।”

In the result, both the Rules in Writ Petition No. 1787 of 1998 and Writ Petition No. 2259 of 1998 are discharged without any order as to costs. The order of stay granted earlier in both Rules is hereby vacated.

End.

Md Fazlul Karim J: These Rules are taken up for hearing together and disposed of by the Single Judgment as the common question of law and facts are involved.

2. The petitioner in Writ Petition No. 2419 of 1998 has impugned Memo No. 375 Justice-7/2N-144/77 dated 2-8-98 Annexure 'A' issued by the respondent No.2 to have been issued without any lawful authority stating, inter alia, that by the impugned order ward No. 5 of Mymensingh Pourashava has been curtailed unlawfully from the Nikah Registry area of the petitioner contrary to the provision of law and rules as the petitioner has been permanently appointed as the Nikah Registrar, for No. 2 Sankipara, No. 8 Akna Unions on 13-6-75 and for No. 1 Kachijhuli, No. 4 Nutanbazar and No. 5 Amlapara Union of Mymensingh Pourashava. The Rule has been contested by filing affidavit-in-opposition by respondent No. 1 who denied all the allegations in the rule application stating, inter alia that the area has been lawfully curtailed as the respondent has authority under section 4 of the Muslim Marriages & Divorces (Registration), Act 1974 to extend, curtail or otherwise alter the limitation of any area for which a Nikah Registrar has been licensed by the Government. The petitioner presently is the Nikah Registrar of Ward Nos. 1, 2 & 3 of Mymensingh Pourashava in accordance with 'the requirement of the laws and the rules.

3. The respondent No.4 filed affidavit-in-opposition denying the allegations in the Rule application and asserted that the curtailment was lawfully done and respondent No.4 was legally appointed Nikah registrar for the curtailed area.

4. In Writ Petition No. 2037 of 1998 the Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondent to show cause as to why the Review Petition dated 28-12-97 (Annexure 'D') should not be disposed of expeditiously stating, inter alia, that the petitioner was a permanent Nikah Registrar for Ward Nos.15, 16, 17 of Dhaka City Corporation which were subsequently renumbered as Ward Nos. 46, 47 and 48. Upon the allegation of solemnisation of marriage of a minor couple notice was issued to him to show cause as to why his licence shall not be revoked. The petitioner showed cause but ultimately the licence was revoked by a notification dated 1-12-93. Whereupon the petitioner filed a review application before the respondent on 28-12-93 under Rule 8(6) of the Muslim Family law. During the pendency of the review petition when he has been functioning as a Nikah Registrar he came to know from a reliable source that ward No. 47 has been taken out of his jurisdiction by an office order passed on 1-7-98 and respondent No. 4 has been temporarily appointed Nikah Registrar for that ward (The copy of which is annexed as Annexure-F). Though the petitioner as Nikah Registrar is entitled to retain a minimum of 3 wards, the respondent has illegally taken away the ward No. 47. The Rille has been contested by the respondent No. 1 denying the allegation in rule application and asserting, inter alia, that the petitioner was never a permanent Nikah Registrar for ward Nos. 46, 47 and 48 but his appointment was of temporary nature and due to misconduct in discharge of his duty his licence was revoked following the procedure provided under law and, as such, the statement/assertion making an application for review was denied and the concerned authority never received the same. The petitioner could not show any paper that the said review application was ever filed or the order of revocation was ever stayed or after the revocation he was appointed afresh or that his review application is still pending. The petitioner also has not taken any step during the last 5 years after revocation of his licence. Any alleged functioning of the petitioner as Nikah Registrar is wholly unauthorised and illegal and alleged deposit of money in the treasury does not make the petitioner a Nikah Registrar. It is not the District Registrar but the Government respondent Nos. 1 and 2 who are the authority to grant licence to Nikah Registrar or revoke the same. The Government never withdrew the order revoking the licence of the petitioner. Any alleged letter by the District Registrar terming the petitioner as Nikah registrar of Rayer Bazar could not revalidate the revoked licence. The respondent No. 4 has been appointed Nikah Registrar for ward No. 47 as the petitioner was not the Nikah registrar. So the question of taking away of ward No. 47 from the jurisdiction of the petitioner does not arise and no such review petition was ever filed or still remaining pending.

5. The respondent No. 4 is contesting the Rule denying the allegation in the rule application and supported the assertions of respondent No.1.

The petitioner in Writ Petition No. 2568 of 1998 has challenged impugned Memo No. 347/1(8) Justice-7/2N-116/87/dated 21-7-98 Annexure 'A' issued under the signature of the respondent No.2 as should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and of no legal effect stating, inter alia, that No. 15 Maitvanga and No.16 Sharikaite Unions have been curtailed unlawfully from the Nikah Registrry area of the petitioner. The said Rule was contested by the respondent No. 4 denying the allegation and stating, inter alia, that under the provisions of law the Government is entitled to extend, curtail or otherwise alter the limit of any area of Nikah Registrar and as such the curtailment of Union No. 5 Maitvanga and No.16 Sharikaite Unions have been done lawfully and in accordance with law and rules and has appointed the respondent No.4 as the Nikah Registrar for those area. The petitioner being an agent entitling himself to the commission was not entitled to any show cause notice prior to curtailment of the area from his original area.

The petitioner in Writ Petition No. 1811 of 1998 has impugned orders contained in Memo No. 265- Bichar-7/2N-96(part) darted 16-6-98 Annexure 'D' and Memo No. 216217 dated  23-6-98 Annexure D(1) and Memo No. 223-Bichar-7/2N- 20176 dated 7-6-98 Annexure 'E' and Memo No. 204717 dated 10-6-98 Annexure-E(1) and Memo No. 51 Bichar-7/2N-297 dated 11-2-98 Annexure-F' and Memo No. 482(7) dated 12-2-98 Annexure- F(1) issued by the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 respectively as have been issued without lawful authority stating, inter alia, in an application under Article 102 of the Constitution that the petitioner was granted licence as Nikah Registrar for all the wards of Khilgaon Union and Rajarbag. Union under Dhaka City by the Chairman of the said Unions. The petitioner was also granted licence as Nikah Registrar for East Tejgaon, West Tegaon, Nowabpur, Dilkusha and part of Kamalapur Unions. The Government also appointed the petitioner as Divorce Registrar for the said Unions with the coming into operation of Muslim Marriage and Divorce (Registration Act 1974) and the petitioner was grantal licence as Nikah Registrar for the aforesaid area. After reconstitution of the area into wards of the Dhaka Municipal Corporation, the petitioner was given ward Nos. 59, 61, 62, 64, 65, 66 and 67. Subsequently ward No. 58 was taken away in exchange of Ward No. 59. The Ward Nos. 59, 61, 62 and 64 to 67 were subsequently re-constituted as wards Nos. 36, 35, 23, 57, 53, 54 and 55. The respondent No. 2 has curtailed the area of the petitioner by taking away wards No. 33 from his area subsequently as well the respondent has curtailed the area of the petitioner by takering away wards No. 35 and 36 from the petitioner and appointed the respondent Nos. 5 and 6 as Nikah Registrars. The rule has been contested by one of the newly appointed Nikah Registrars, the respondent No.5, denying the allegations in the rule application stating, inter alia, that the curtailment was made legally and the respondent No.5 was given ward No. 35 to Act as the Nikah Registrar for the area.

The petitioner in Writ Petition No. 4135 of 1998 has impugned Memo No. 8057(7) dated 20-9-98 Annexure-A issued under the signature of respondent No. 3 as to why it should not be declared to have been made without any lawful authority and of no legal effect stating, inter alia, in an application under Article 102 of the Constitution that by the impugned Memo some parts of Santahar (Ka) and the whole of Santahar (Kha) Unions presently constituting the Santahar Pourashava has been curtailed unlawfully from the Nikah Registry area of the petitioners as the petitioner has been appointed as Nikah Registrar for the 7 Union Parishads including the curtailed area.

The petitioner in Wlit Petition No. 3716 of 1998 has impugned the memo No. 1291(6) dated 21-10-98 Annexure A issued under the signature of respondent No. 3 as should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority stating inter alia, in an application under Article 102 of the Constitution. that the petitioner was permanently appointed Nikah Registrar for No.16 Goalbari Union under PS Kulaura District Sylhet on 9-3-85, 5 Unions namely, No. 11 Sharifpur, No. 12 Prithimpashas No. 13 Karmada, No. 14 Fultala and No. 15 Sagarnal under Kulaura PS have been annexed to his registrar, But by the impugned memo ward No. 12 of Parithirnpasha Union has been unlawfully curtailed from the Nikah Registrar area of the Writ Petitioner without any opportunity of being heard.

The petitioner in Writ Petition No. 3313 of 1998 has impugned Memo No. 877(10) dated 13-10-98 Annexure A stating, inter-alia; in an application under Article 102 of the Constitution that by the impugned Memo No. 877(10) dated 13-10-98 under the signature of the respondent No. 3 by which MadIa Union has been curtailed unlawfully from the Nikah Registry area of the petitioner although the petitioner was licensed for Sultangonj, Lahiripara, Sheikhercola, Shakharia, Subgram, Rajapur and Maykira including the MadIa Union by a licence dated 9-9-86. The Rule has been contested by the respondent No. 4 denying allegations in the application stilting, inter alia, that the curtailment was done in accordance with law and respondent No.4 was lawfully appointed as the Nikah Registrar.

52. In the backdrop of the aforesaid submissions it appears that the Bengal Act I, of 1876 namely, The Bengal Mohammadan Marriages and Divorces Registration Act 1876 has provided provision for the voluntary registration of marriages and divorces among Mohammdans, under section 3 thereof. It was lawful for the Provincial Government to grant a licence to any person being a Mohammadan authorising him to register Mohammadan marriages and divorces which have been effected within certain specified limits on an application being made to him for such registration and in like manner it shall be lawful for the Provisional Government to revoke or sustain such licence, provided that not more than two persons shall be licenced to exercise the said function within the same limit. Thus the Government was authorised to grant licence to any person to register Muslim marriages and divorces within certain specified limit.

53. By Kazi Act of 1880 the Government was empowered to appoint one and more Kazis for such local area as the Government may think fit for solemnising the marriages or performance of any rite or ceremony. With the introduction of Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961, section 5 thereof provided for granting licence by the Chairman of the Union Parishad for the local area to act as the Marriage Registrar. The said provision of section 5 has been omitted by Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Act of 1974 (LII of 1974) providing section 4 thereof that for the purpose of the registration of marriages, the Government snail grant licence to such number of persons, to be called Nikah Registrars, as it may deem necessary, for such areas as may specify, provided that not more than one Nikah Registrar shall be licensed for any one area. The Muslim Marriage and Divorce Registration (Amendment) Ordinance 1982 which came into force on 1st December, 1992 amended the said section 4 introducing a proviso that provided further that the Government may whenever deems fit so to do extend, curtail or otherwise alter the limit of any area of which a Nikah Registrar has been licensed. Under section 14 thereof, Rules have been framed for carrying out the purpose of the said Act being Muslim Marriages and Divorce (Registration) Rules, 1975 providing for proceedings including Jurisdiction in rule 10 whereby it has provided area for which a Nikah Registrar may be licensed shall be the whole area of a Pourashava or 5 to 10 constituencies of a Municipal Corporation or 5 to 10 Unions as may be recommended by the Advisory Committee. The said rule 10 has further been substituted by notification dated 14, December, 1982 providing the area a Nikah Registrar may be licensed shall be:

a) in the case of Municipality

(i) if it is under a Municipal Corporation not more than the areas of five wards;

(ii) if it is in a district headquarter, not more than the area of eight wards; and

(iii) if otherwise, not more than the areas to which that Municipality extends; and

(b) in other cases, not more than the areas of 10 Unions; The said provision has further undergone substitution by notification dated 19-1-93 providing that the area for which a Nikah Registrar may be licensed shall be:

(a) in the case of a Municipal Corporation: 2-4 wards

(b) in the case of other Municipalities, 3-5 wards; and

(c) in other cases, 3-5 Unions.

In sub-rule 10(2) it has been provided that the provision of sub-rule (i) shall not affect the area of a Nikah Registrar licensed immediately before the commencement of that sub-rule until he is retired or his office otherwise falls vacant. The said rule has further been substituted by notification dated 30' December, 1997 providing as under:

"10. jurisdiction. The area for which a Nikah Registrar may be licensed shall be:

(a) in the case of an area under a City Corporation or Pourashava, not more than 3 wards.

(b) in the case of other areas, not more than 3 unions.

54. In view of increasing number of populations and widening delimitation of the Paura Corporation Municipal area and Unions incorporating more areas/wards and in order to facilitate registration of marriages and divorces, which are increasing day by day, the legislature has amended the provision of Act, 1974 incorporating in 2nd proviso to section 4 as above mentioned and in order to carry out the purposes of the Act has framed rules and substituted rule 10 being the jurisdiction of each Nikah Registrar for effective easy and smooth registration of the marriages and divorces in any particular area.

<u>55. With the introduction of the said and proviso to section 4 of the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Act of 1974, rules for carrying out the purpose and object of the Act were amended and substituted from time.to time-Section 6(c) of the General Clauses Act. 1897 has no application thereto as there was no repeal of any enactment. In the present case there has been amendments/substitution to effect the jurisdiction of the Nikah Registrar area and such amendment/substitution can not be put at par with the repeal of a statute with or without a saving clause. The 2nd proviso to section 4 authorises the Government to extend, curtail or otherwise alter the limit of any area for which a Nikah Registrar has been licensed. Rule 10(2) of the Rules 1975 as amended in 1995 provides for the area for which a Nikah Registrar maybe licensed in the case of Municipal Corporation-three to four wards, in the case of other Municipal Corporations three to five wards and in other cases, three to five unions, but rule 10(2) operates as a stumbling block in the exercise of power under 2nd proviso to section 4 of the Act as although said section empowered the Government to extend, curtail or otherwise alter the limit of any area of a Nikah Registrar, the said power can not be exercised in respect of the Nikah Registrar licensed immediately before the commencement of the sub-rule until he is retired or his office has otherwise fallen vacant This anomaly in the sub-rule (2) can he answered by resorting to the rule of interpretation that the rule having been framed to carry out the purpose. and object of the Act itself, if operates as a block and as such the rule to that extent is void and accordingly sub-rule (2) rule 10 of the Rules of 1975 must be held to be void. In other words, where there arises controversy between the power of rule making authority and that of the legislature, it is the rule of construction of the statute that the enactment shall control the rule. Thus the rule making authority could not exceed its power in derogation to the power, of legislative enactment. The Appellate Division in the case ef Kazi Md Amirul lslam vs Secretary, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Bangladesh and others reported in, 16 BLD (AD) 110 where the petitioner was appointed as Nikah Registrar of Shirajpur, Char Purbali and Char Hazar Unions but Government declared some parts of those Unions to be urban area to form as part of Basurhat Pourashava for which the Government. subsequently decided to issue licence to the Nikah Registrar and asked the petitioner as to whether he would like to continue to exercise jurisdiction, as Nikah Registrar within the three Unions or to act as such for Basurhat Pourashava and the petitioner opted for the three Unions. But he challenged the order of the Government dated 19-12-93 appointing respondent No. 4 aa Nikah Registrar for Basurhat Pourashava in the areas which had been previously part of the aforesaid three Unions referring rule 10(2) of the Muslim Marriages and Divorce (Registration) Rufes 1975 as amended by notification dated 19-1-93 and on the submission of the learned Advocate-on-record that in view of the provision of Rule 10(2) of the Muslim Marriages and Divorce (Registration) Rules 1975 as amended on 19-1-93 the petitioner was entitled to exercise his jurisdiction as Marriage Registrar for the area which were previously part Of the aforesaid three Unions until he is retired or his office otherwise falls vacant, it was held that the learned Judges Of the High Court Division elaborately discussed Rule 10 of the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Rules, 1975 as amended and rightly held that the Government had the power to alter, extend, curtail or otherwise alter the limits of any such Union for which a Nikah Registrar has been licensed to exercise his jurisdiction. The learned Judges further rightly held that there is no dispute that the Government is competent to curtail the jurisdiction of any Union and declare any part of it as an 'Urban area' and thereafter include the said area in a Paurashava and, as such, the territories of the above three Unions have been curtailed lawfully and included within the Bashurhat Paurashava which cannot be considered as parts of those three Unions and the petitioner therefore, cannot claim to exercise his jurisdiction over the areas of the aforesaid three Unions which have been Included within the Bashurhat Pourashava. As such; there is no substance in the contention of the learned Advocate-on-Record. The petition is dismissed. The judgment by the- Appellate Division was delivered dated 14-1-96. When sub-rule 10(2) was in force but though the Appellate Division did, not declare the same as ultra vires of the Act instead, ignored the same. Siinilarly in a subsequent decision in the case of Mostafa Kamal Moulvi Mohammad Khorshed vs Secretary Ministry of Law Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, reported in 50 DLR (AD) 82 on a fact the Government by order dated 25-10-95 appointed respondent No.   5 Md Rabiul Haque Patwary as Nikah Registrar in respect of newly constituted Amjadhat Union within Fulgazi Union by curtailing under section 4 of the Act of 1974 the Nikah Registry area of the petitioner who challenged the same alleging his appointment as Nikah Registrar in respect of 4 Unions including Amjadhat Union in 1991 and under sub-rule 10(2) such curtailment of area from his Nikah Registrar is not permissible and being a Nikah Registrar is entitled to work for such area including Amjadhat Union until he retires or his office otherwise falls vacant, held in the similar manner that the second proviso to the said section 4 has empowered the Government to extend, curtail or otherwise alter the limits of any area for which a Nikah Registrar has been licensed whenever the Government deems fit to do so. The decision further held that the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that such curtailment of area from the Nikah Registrar area of the petitioner amounts to revocation of his licence so far Amjadhat Union is concerned is not acceptable inasmuch as it is not a case of revocation of licence contemplated in rule 8 of the Rules. It is a case of curtailment of Nikah Registration areas under section 4 of the Act. Rule 10(2) was taken notice of while delivering the judgment on 20th November 1997. The Government has further substituted the entire Rule 10 including 10(2) on 31 December 1997 by the present Rule which does not contain any provision like sub-Rule 2 of Rule 10 and provided that the area for which a Nikah Registrar may be licensed shall be in the case of an area under a city corporation or pourashava not more than three wards; and in the case of other areas, not more than three Unions. The impugned orders in the rules under consideration are almost all of the dates after the present amendment in 1997. The Nikah Registrars were appointed either temporarily or permanently to register the marriages for and on behalf of the Government. They register the marriages/divorces for or on behalf of the Government in the specified area of their jurisdiction. Although they were issued licences, their position are no a better than those of the licensee in respect of land or building and the licence thus issued confer on a person the right to do something which otherwise he would not have legal power to do, which is a special privilege rather than-a right common to all and is often required as a condition precedent to the right to carryon business or to hold certain classes of property within the jurisdiction and, as such, they do not acquire any vested right so as to be entitled to a prior notice to show cause before the curtailment of the area of their operation.</u>

56. In view of the above including the effect of substitution, no vested right has been accrued to the petitioners and the submission that the said right could not retrospectively be taken away has no substance. In the case of Mr.Raisuddin vs Secretary Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs in Writ Petition No. 1744 of 1998, in an unreported decision on a similar fact. Mr Justice AM Mahmudur Rahman (as his Lordships then was) has observed, inter alia, that in the fact of the present case there accrued no vested right and no vested right has been taken away retrospectively by the impugned order and relied in the case of Kazi Amirul Islam which held that the Government is competent to curtail the jurisdiction of any union and declare any part of it as an urban area and further observed that "Dr. Kamal Hossain urged that the amendment was intended to secure the interest of the public at large and by the impugned orders such interest has been secured although the right of the petitioners to exercise his function by the orders impugned has been narrowed down. Dr Hossain says that such reduction is not and cannot be an absolute deprivation of the right of the petitioner. In my opinion the legislature is to secure benefit for the people or in otherwise. the legislation is a beneficial one and the amendment was introduced to give effect to the policy of the Government to secure benefit to more persons as the amendment also is not to the total deprivation of the petitioner's right to function as a Nikah Registrar but it has narrowed down the limit of his area of activity."

<u>57. Mr Razzak has referred to a decision in the case of Md Aftabuddin vs Government of Bangladesh in an unreported decision in Writ Petition No. 2136 of 1994 in whichone of us was a party wherein the curtailment contrary to rule 10(2) was declared without lawful authority. The said decision dated 6-12-95 was prior to the decisions of the Appellate Division and the said decision on the fact did not consider the effect of rule 10(2) upon section 4 of the Act and the said decisions have been superseded by the decision of the Appellate Division and, as such, has no application in the instant case. Rule 5A of Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Rules 1975 though provided that notwithstanding anything contained in rule 5 any person acting as Nikah Registrar on temporary basis under rule 5(1) on the commencement of this Rule (19-1-93) and have completed 2 years as .such, subject to the provision of rule 10 shall be granted licence as Nikah Registrar if after scrutiny of his qualification; certificates and records the advisory committee finds that he fulfils the requisite qualification specified in rule 6 and his performance during the period of holding temporary licence is satisfactory. The said rule 6 has been framed providing for qualification to be required from persons to whom a licence under section 4 may be granted. Rule 5 of the Rules 1975 provides for selection of candidate i.e. on the occurrence of a vacancy or on the creation of a new office of Nikah Registrar, the Registrar may with the approval of the Government issue licence to a qualified person to act as Nikah Registrar on purely temporary basis until a Nikah Registrar is licensed by Government on regular basis and invite application for the purpose. Upon receipt of the application the same shall be placed before the Advisory Committee for consideration and selection of candidates. The qualification of the candidates have been enumerated in rule 6 and shall process the same through the Advisory Committee, Thus under the rule 5A a Nikah Registrar is entitled to a licence upon completion of 2 years period as temporary Nikah Registrar for the permissible area having requisite qualification, duly recommended by the Advisory Committee. It may be mentioned that a Nikah Registrar appointed temporarily for the permissible area is also liable to be accorded with a licence by the Government by publishing the same in the official gazette through being processed by the Advisory Committee. The licence so granted empowers the Nikah Registrar to act on behalf of the Government to register marriage or divorce in lieu of fees to the Government and the Nikah Registrar receiving the commission only. Thus a Nikah Registrar, in effect is an agent of the Government and the Nikah Registrar's licence is also liable to be revoked, suspended, annulled following the procedure provided under rule 8 thereof. Be that as it may, the Government has authority to curtail, extend or otherwise alter the limit of any Nikah Registrar within the permissible-limit of area without any notice, even in the case of permanent Nikah Registrar.</u>

<u>58. In view of the above, neither the principle of natural justice nor question of vested right arises in the way of passing an order for curtailment of the area of jurisdiction of the petitioner within the permissible limit of area.</u>

59. In view of the above, the impugned orders did not suffer for any illegality warranting our interference.

60. In the result, these Rules are discharged without any order as to costs.

The order of stay granted by this court earlier in the above Rules, are hereby vacated.

End.

lawyer:
Dr M Zahir with Md Firoz Shah with AHM Mizanur Rahman and Afreen Mohiuddin, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner.

parties:
American Express Bank Limited ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Chairman National Board of Revenue and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Munsurul Hoque Chowdhury J: Supplementary affidavits filed on behalf of the petitioner be made part of the record.

2. This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned letter dated 22-6-1998 of the respondent No. 3 re-opening income tax cases of the petitioner for six years from 1992-93 to 1997-98 (Annexure-I) and the continuation of the said proceedings as evidenced by notices of respondent No. 3 dated 16-7-1998 (Annexure-K, K1, K2, K3, K4, and K5) shall not be declared to have been made without any lawful authority and of no legal effect.

3. Facts relevant for disposal of the Rule are that the petitioner a banking institution incorporated in the State of Connecticut, USA having its head office located in New York City, New York State, USA, The petitioner company being a banking company operates branches in different countries of the world including branches in Bangladesh through banking licence obtained on 29th June 1965 under the Banking Companies Ordinance 1962 to conduct banking business in Dhaka with a foreign-exchange licence dated 5th September 1972 under the Foreign Exchange Regulations Act, 1947. The petitioner company has its branches in different cities of Bangladesh under proper and valid authorities. Until 31st December 1975 Head Office expenses which include actual administrative and operative expenses incurred by the petitioner bank in New York for its branches in Bangladesh were allowed by Bangladesh Bank to be separately repatriated but the same was subsequently disallowed from 1st January 1976 and the item "Head Office expenses" could no longer be reflected in the profit and loss account of American Express Bank Bangladesh (petitioner) but the said Head Office expenses being incurred and claimed by the Head Office for business purpose the petitioner demanded for exemption of corporate tax on this particular Head in its Income Tax return. As Head Office expenses chargeable on the petitioner for branches in Bangladesh by the head office in New York the petitioner debited the amount as "Head Office expenses" in its books of account for the tax assessment year 1989-90 as was done in earlier years. The petitioner submitted tax return along with its profit and loss account as required to be filed in Bangladesh according to banking rules and in the said profit and loss account the expenditure incurred by Head Office was not shown but the same amount was shown in the total computation sheet of Income and Tax liability attached with the return.

4. In income tax return for assessment year 1980-90 the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes refused to allow New York Head Office expenses for the Tax assessment year 1989-90 and against the same petitioner went on appeal before the Appellate Joint Commissioner of Taxes who after hearing of the parties allowed the "Head Office expenses" as deductible expense and against the said order, the Deputy Commissioner Taxes preferred appeal to the Taxes Appellate Tribunal being ITA No. 1218 of 1990-91 (assessment year 1989-90). The Taxes Appellate Tribunal then by judgment and order dated 2-8-1994 upheld the petitioner's contention that Head Office expenses made by New York Head Office for the business to its Bangladesh office would be a deductible expense in Bangladesh and the decision having been accepted by the Income Tax Department the same was not referred to the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh for further adjudication. Position being such on appeal the petitioner continued to submit assessment returns showing Head Office expenses in the total computation sheet without referring the amount in the profit and loss account sheet and in assessment year namely, for the year 1990-91 and assessment year 1991-92 Tax assessment returns were submitted to the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes showing the Head Office expenses in the total computation sheet duly certified by the chartered accountant and the same were accepted and assessed by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes without putting any objection to the total computation sheet. Then accordingly, the petitioner company on subsequent assessment years 1992-93, 1993-94, 1994-95, 1995-96, 1996-97 and 1997-98 submitted Income Tax returns before the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes within time along with profit and loss account duly certified by the chartered accountant accompanied by total computation sheet of Income Tax liability showing therewith the Head Office expenses and in all the assessment years the assessment returns were duly certified by the chartered accountant and accompanied by certificate of the chartered accountant as required under law and on being satisfied with the returns submitted by the petitioner in all the years of assessment were accepted by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes holding that the Income Tax returns submitted showing profit and loss were duly examined and certified by the Chartered Accountant as required under section 82 of Income Tax Ordinance. Suddenly the petitioner received a letter from respondent No. 3 on 22-6-1998 purported to have acted with the approval of respondent No. 2 under section 93 of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984 calling upon the petitioner to file fresh returns for the assessment years from 1992-93 to 1997-98 alleging that in those returns the petitioner though shown to have deducted Head Office expenses in total Income Tax computation sheet but did not disclose the basis of making such deduction for Head Office expenses and the sources of money for financing such expenses did not reflect in the profit and loss account sheet which according to respondent No. 3 resulted in under assessment for those years in question and the petitioner was thus served with notice to submit returns afresh for those years in dispute within 21 days. On receipt of said notices the tax adviser of the petitioner by letter dated 9-7-1998 protested the reopening of file mentioning that the Taxes Appellate Tribunal has already decided the issue and thus the respondent No. 3 cannot now reopen the same. The respondent No.3 ignoring the protest of the petitioner served notice upon the petitioner on 16-7-1998 under section 83 (1) of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984 for all the 6 years stating that statement of account were not submitted with the returns and expenses are not comparable and wanted the petitioner to show cause by 30-7-1998 as to why returns should not be rejected. On such premises of the case the petitioner moved this court challenging the legality of the notices served under section 93 of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984 and obtained the present Rule.

5. Respondent No. 1 appeared in the Rule by filing affidavit-in-opposition and supplementary affidavit-in-opposition and reply. It is the case of the respondent that the validity of notices served under section 93 of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984 cannot be called in question as in response to such notice the petitioner has already submitted the returns. It is then stated that the petitioner stopped disclosing the Head Office expenses in its profit and loss account and kept on remitting the said amount to the Head Office under cover of profit. It is further stated that when it came to the notice of the Deputy Commissioner, Taxes that Head Office expenses so shown in the total competition sheet not being reflected in the profit and loss account sheet the same required to be examined as to the basis of such deduction. An assessee is entitled to deduction of any expense incurred for earning income which is subject to income tax but the expenditure must pass through books of account and consequently through the final account and balance sheet and since the final account and the balance sheet certified by its Auditors did not contain any debit for any expense by Head Office and since the petitioner resorted to deducting large sums of money in the name of Head Office expenses in the total computation sheet in a fishy manner by passing the books of accounts, the manner of such attempt justified the reopening of the cases as mentioned above. It is further stated that the petitioner is entitled to deduction of any expenditure upon fulfillment of conditions that the expenditure has been incurred and is definite and it has been incurred, wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business but the petitioner did not furnish any evidence whatsoever that the deduction made in the computation sheet on Account of Head Office expenses were definite and actually incurred and they were incurred wholly and exclusively for the purpose of business in Bangladesh. It is then stated that section 82 of Income Tax Ordinance 1984 provides for acceptance of returns as correct and complete if the return is accompanied by certificate of Chartered Accountant in prescribed form under rule 64A of Income Tax Rules 1984 but in the instant case no such certificate was enclosed as per rule 64A of the Income Tax Rule 1984. It is also stated that a huge amount of money was claimed as Head Office expenses without showing the basis as the same is not allowable under clause XXVII to section 29(1) of the Income Tax Ordinance.

6. Dr M Zahir, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, has submitted at the outset that where the Taxes Appellate Tribunal has allowed the Head Office expenses deductible in the case of assessment year 1989-90 and the said decision having not been challenged by the Income Tax Department and for 2 subsequent years of assessment namely, assessment year 1990-91, assessment year 1991-92 the assessment returns were accepted allowing Head Office expenses, the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes was not justified calling in question the basis of deduction of Head Office expenses after lapse of 6 assessment years by reopening of the cases exercising power under section 93 of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984. He then submitted the notices impugned are illegal and without jurisdiction as the same does not come within the scope of section 93 of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984. He further submitted that once Income Tax returns were accepted by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes and were found to be correct with all required particulars, the same cannot be reopened for the purpose of re-assessment claiming the returns were submitted showing under assessment. He lastly submitted that since there was no non-disclosure of facts, the respondent No. 3 was not entitled to serve a notice invoking power under section 93 of Income Tax Ordinance 1984 directing the petitioner to file fresh returns.

7. Mr Dabir Uddin Ahmed, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the respondent No. 1, has submitted at the very outset that the writ petition is not maintainable as equally efficacious remedy is available in the law itself as the petitioner could have approached the superior authority of the said department under section 121 of the said Ordinance. It is then submitted that though the Head Office expenses were shown in the total computation sheet but the same ought to have been shown in the profit and loss account sheet with break up showing the basis of such expenses and the same having not been done is a non-disclosure and the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes has committed no illegality in issuing notice upon the petitioner under section 93 of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984 asking to furnish fresh return for those years. Lastly, he has, submitted that the returns were not duly certificated by the chartered accountant as required under prescribed form 64A of the Income Tax Rules 1984. Therefore, certificate, if any, cannot be construed as certificate under rule 64A of Income Tax Rules 1984.

8. Dr M Zahir has taken us through the writ petition, the affidavit-in-opposition and supplementary affidavit including the annexures. Referring to Annexure A to the writ petition. the learned Advocate for the petitioner has submitted that for the assessment year 1989-90 the petitioner submitted Income Tax returns with profit and loss accounts accompanied by a total computation sheet of Income Tax and liabilities and in the total computation sheet a lump amount of Head Office expenses incurred during that assessment year was shown but the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes refused to accept the Head Office expenses shown in the total computation sheet as deductible Income and same was challenged by way of appeal and the appellate authority allowed the Head Office expenses as deductible income. Against the said appellate order the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes preferred further appeal before the Taxes Appellate Tribunal who also held that the Head Office expenses is an allowable expenditure deductible from the Income of the petitioner. We have gone through the judgment of the Taxes Appellate Tribunal, Annexure- B to the writ petition and found that the Taxes Appellate Tribunal held that the Head Office expenses shown in the total computation sheet was not for the purpose of avoiding taxes and the same was allowed. We do not find from the affidavit-in-opposition and the learned Deputy Attorney-General also did not dispute that the judgment and order of the Taxes Appellate Tribunal was not reversed by any competent superior court. In our view, the respondents are thus stopped from disputing over the claim of Head Office expenses without disturbing the Judgment of the Tax Appellate Tribunal. Annexures- C-H are the disputed Income Taxes returns for the assessment period from 1992-93 to 1997-98. It appears from all of the assessment returns that all those returns were accompanied by certificates from the Chartered Accountant and the total computation sheet also includes Head Office expenses incurred during the years of assessment.

<u>9. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has submitted that this Head Office expenses were not shown in the profit and loss account sheet and the same were also not shown in profit and loss account sheet for the previous assessment years. He has then drawn our attention by submitting that according to second proviso of section 82 of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984, the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes is made to assess the return filed by the assessee if accompanied by certified copy of account of the assessee audited by a chartered accountant and a certificate as to the correctness of the total Income of the assessee is signed and issued by the chartered accountant himself in the prescribed form. From all the disputed Income Tax returns it appears that the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes assessed the Income of the petitioner accepting the returns holding that the Income Tax returns submitted were duly audited and certified as required under section 82 of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984. This being the consistent finding of the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes and authorised officer in all the cases, it cannot be said after lapse of years that the returns were not submitted properly, correctly or in accordance with the requirements of law and the question of basis of showing Head Office expenses should not be allowed to be raised. It is the basic requirement of second proviso of section 82 of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984 that before acceptance of return the assessee will satisfy the authority that the profit and loss account sheet has duly been audited by a chartered accountant and the same was accompanied by a certificate in a prescribed form issued by the same chartered accountant. We have already found from the order of the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes in all the returns that after due consideration and examination of papers submitted with the Income Tax returns the same were accepted. If there would be any illegality or irregularity apparent, the same could have been raised by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes before accepting those returns. From the impugned Annexure it appears that the notice under section 93 of the Income Tax Ordinance was served upon the petitioner on the ground that the Head Office expenses were shown in total computation sheet but the basis of making such deduction for Head Office expenses was not shown in the profit and loss account sheet, this, according to the respondent No. 3, was underassessment. Section 93 of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984 is applicable only in 3 cases. Notice for reopening of Income Tax return can be made where income chargeable to tax for any assessment year has escaped assessment or has been under assessed or has been assessed at too low rate for excessive relief or refund under the Ordinance. From the disputed Annexure-C-H, it appears, the Head Office expenses though not shown in the profit and loss account sheet but was shown in the total computation sheet duly audited and certified by a chartered accountant as required under second proviso of section 82 of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984. This non-mentioning of Head Office expenses in profit and loss account sheet cannot be termed as a non- disclosure or has been done for escaping assessment nor this manner of disclosure can be said to be underassessment and were done for any excessive relief. We have already found that Head Office expenses are allowable and deductible expenses from assessment of tax. In our view, for non-mentioning of the same in the profit and loss account sheet shall not make any difference, as the same has already been included in the total Income computation sheet.</u>

<u>10. It may be pointed out here that in the case of returns submitted by a public limited company or anybody corporate established or constituted by or under any law or any other institutions as provided in second proviso of section 82 required to follow the procedure laid down therein and in the instant case the said procedures are found to have been followed at the time of filing of the returns. It also appears from the assessment order passed by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes, in all the disputed assessment years, the returns were found to be in order and no dispute with regard to any formality or requirement was raised before accepting those returns. Further, from second proviso to section 82 it is clear to us that if a return is submitted duly audited by chartered accountant accompanied by a certificate of correctness in prescribed form the same should be taken to be as correct and should be accepted and in the present case following this provision of law the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes had accepted the disputed returns. Once returns are accepted by an authority competent, certifying that the returns are in order, unless otherwise found definite the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes is not competent to serve notice under section 93 of the Ordinance upon the petitioner asking him to submit fresh return holding the returns already assessed and accepted as under assessed.</u>

11. The next point raised by Mr Dabir Uddin Ahmed, the learned Deputy Attorney-General, was that certificates as required to be furnished were not so furnished by the chartered accountant in prescribed form as in rule 64A of Income Tax Rules 1984. In this connection the learned advocate for the petitioner has taken us through the Annexure- Y2 to the supplementary affidavit which is a certificate given under the hand of chartered accountant in assessment return for assessment year 1991-92. Showing this Annexure the learned Advocate for the petitioner has submitted that similar certificates were also enclosed with all the Income Tax assessment returns for all subsequent years including the disputed assessment years. We have compared the certificate given in Annexure-Y2 with the prescribed form shown in Income Tax Manual. We do not find any variation of language in the prescribed form with that of the certificate issued by the chartered accountant. Though it is asserted by the learned Deputy Attorney-General that certificates in prescribed forms were not enclosed with the Income Tax returns of the disputed years but he could not produce those certificates to substantiate his this field of argument. Time was allowed to the learned Deputy Attorney-General to produce the relevant assessment returns of the disputed assessment years but the same were not brought before us for our satisfaction. Since it is alleged by the learned Deputy Attorney-General that the certificates enclosed with the disputed returns were not in prescribed form onus is verily upon the claimant to prove the contention by producing those disputed certificates but in the absence of such certificates it is unsafe for us to hold that the certificates issued by the chartered accountant were not in prescribed forms. On the other hand, from Annexures-C-H the disputed returns with the assessment order show that the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes perused the certificates and found the same to be correct. Thus the submission made by the learned Deputy Attorney-General on this point does not have any substance.

12. On the point of disclosure of basis of Head Office expenses it was submitted by the learned Deputy Attorney-General that although in total computation sheet a lump amount was shown as Head Office expenses but the said amount was not shown in profit and loss amount sheet with break-up showing the basis of such amount. In this regard Dr M Zahir has drawn our attention to Annexure-X series from which he has shown to us, the Head Office expenses as shown in the total computation sheet of the disputed years were on the basis of the description provided by the Head Office of the petitioner for each particular year of assessment. We have compared the amounts shown in the total computation sheets of disputed assessment years with the Annexure-X series and also of the amount shown in 3 successive previous years from assessment year 1989-90 to 1991-92. It appears to us the amount shown in all the years as Head Office expenses are almost nearer to the amount shown in assessment year 1989-90 which went up to the Taxes Appellate Tribunal, which also allowed Taka 1,43,58,278 as Head Office expenses. Further, the description with breakup showing Head Office expenses shown in Annexure-X series for the disputed years of assessment has not been denied or controverted to the effect that the same were not shown to the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes during the relevant assessment years. As no contrary fact could have been placed before us by the learned Deputy Attorney-General in support of his contention we do not find any reason to keep those Annexure-X series out of our consideration.

<u>13. The next question as raised by the learned Deputy Attorney-General is, that the writ petition is not maintainable as there is alternative efficacious remedy available in the Ordinance itself and in advancing his argument on this point the learned Deputy Attorney-General has referred to section 121 of the Income Tax Ordinance and has submitted that if the petitioner was so aggrieved by the impugned notice he could have approached the Commissioner for revising the order but without approaching the Commissioner, he has invoked the jurisdiction of this court under Article 102 of the Constitution which, according to him, is not maintainable. In reply to such submissions, the learned Advocate for the petitioner has submitted that since the very basis of issuance of notice under section 93 of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984 is under challenge on the ground of want of jurisdiction, the petitioner without approaching the Commissioner under section 121 of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984 is entitled to invoke the writ jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution and the writ petition is maintainable. We have already found that the impugned notice served upon the petitioner does not attract requirements of section 93 of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984. We are thus of opinion that the writ petition is maintainable in the present form.</u>

14. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case as discussed above we are of the view that the impugned letter issued by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes vide memo No. 002-200-2391/COY-2/97-98/989 dated 22-6-1998 and subsequent notices under section 83(1) of Income Tax Ordinance 1984 dated 16-7-1998 for assessment years, 1992-93 to 1997-98 are without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

In the result the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs.

End.
