full_judgment:
This Second Appeal by the defendant appellant is against the judgment and decree dated 24.3.1962 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Noakhali in Title Appeal No. 276 of 1960 (reversing those dated 15.9.1960) passed by the learned Munsif, 2nd Court Sudharam, in Title Suit No. 66 of 1952.

2. The respondent as plaintiffs instituted the aforesaid suit for declaration of their title in the disputed lands mentioned in the Schedules 'Ka' and 'Kha' appended to the plaint. They also prayed for Khash possession of the land in the schedule Ka of the plaintiff on removal of the constructions therefrom. During the pendency of the suit the plaintiffs got the plaint amended by inserting a further prayer for recovery of possession of Schedule-Kha lands also.

3. The plaintiffs case, in brief, was that one Maniruddin @ Alirnuddin, father of the defendant No. 1 Nansur Ali took Osat raiyati settlement in respect of 1 Kani 5 gandas of land at an annual rental of Rs. 8/8/- for a period of three years from late Madan Mohan Saha predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs on the basis of a kabuliyat executed on the 9th Jaishtha, 1290 BS. After expiry of the lease period, as under-raiyati right was not heritable, the lands subsequently came in the khas possesion of the landlords. Thereafter the defendant No. 1 and Ramjan Banoo the widow left by the said Maniruddin took settlement of 1'40 acres of land at an annual rental of Rs. 8/8/-. This under-raiyati has been recorded in Khatian No. 25 of Mouza Batra under Khatian No. 24 of the said Mouza. Then Maniruddin and Ramjan Banoo left the village surrendering their under-raiyati lands in favour of the landlords. They went away to a village named Rasulpur and began to live therein. The under-raiyati lands came into the Khas possession of the landlords who began to possess the same in their Khas possession. In 1330 BS one Eusuf Ali, a son-in-law of said Maniruddin took dar-raiyati settlement of 8 gandas of land out of those lands at a jama of Rs. 6/8/- for a period of 9 years. After the death of Eusuf Ali, his heirs being unable to pay rents surrendered the lands in favour of the landlords. In 1330 BS. the defendant No. 1 himself came to the landlords and prayed for settlement of some lands on which the landlords who agreed to lease out some lands to him on condition that he would come over from Rasulpur and reside on the land to be settled with him. Accordingly the defendant No. 1 executed a kabuliyat in favour of the landlords agreed to lease out some lands to him on conditions that he would come over from Rasulpur and reside on the land to be settled with him. Accordingly the 'defendant No. 1 executed a kabuliyat in favour of the landlords on the 28th Poush, 1330 BS. But ultimately the defendant No. 1 did not come over to village Batra from Rasulpur and hence the kabuliyat was not acted upon.

4. Taking advantage of the communal tension prevailing in the country and on being invited by the enemies of the plaintiffs, the defendants trespassed on the Ka schedule land, on the 7th Bhadra, 3358 BS and constructed a dochala hut therein and then constructed another hut. Thus they also dispossessed the plaintiffs from the Kha-Schedule lands. During the pendency of the suit, the plaintiffs prayed for recovery of possession of Kha schedule-lands also on the ground that subsequently they have been dispossessed from those lands of Kha-schedule also. With the above averments, the suit was instuted by the plaintiff.

5. Defendant No. 1 Mansur Ali and defendant No. 4 Mati Miah filed a joint written statement to contest the suit and the guardian-ad-litem appointed for the minor defendant No. 3 also filed another written statement and they also contested the suit. The defendant No. 1 as already stated is a son of the said Maniruddin. The defendant Nos. 2 to 4 are the heirs of one Dula Mia who was a surviving son of Eusuf Ali, the son-in-law of Maniruddin. Their case, in brief, was that Manuruddin did not surrender 1 Kani 5 gandas of land which were taken in under-raiyati settlement by him from Madan Mohan Saha, the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs on the basis of the kabuliyat executed on the 9th Chaitra 1290 BS. On the death of Maniruddin these lands devolved upon his heirs who again executed a fresh kabuliyat in favour of the landlords. The under-raiyati of Maniruddin consisted of CS Plot Nos. 193, 194,195, 202 and -/8/- annas share of CS Plot Nos. 327 and 328. The CS Plot No. 202 and 8 annas share of CS Plot Nos. 327 and 328 have been rightly recorded as appertaining to the under-raiyati of khatian No. 25 but the first three plots namely, plot Nos. 193-195 have been wrongly recorded as khas land of landlords in Khatian No. 24. The heirs of Maniruddin have all along been possessing the under-raiyati lands which belonged to Maniruddin and they have been residing in the homestead which belonged to said Maniruddin. They never left the place and went to Rasulpur for the purpose of their residence. The landlords agreed to settle some lands out of their khas lands. to defendant No.1 for which the defendant No. 1 executed a Kabuliyat in favour of the landlords, which was written by a karmachari of the landlords. That karmachari of the landlords fraudulently inserted some recitals in the kabuliyat stating that the defendant No. 1 surrendered the under-raiyati and had been residing at Rasulpur. Eusuf Ali took settlement of 8 gandas of land appertaining to the Khas-lands of the landlords of khatian No. 24 and the heirs of Eusuf Ali possessing those lands. They did not surrender those lands. Besides the suit was barred by limitation. Hence the suit was liable to be dismissed with cost.

6. The learned Munsif framed the following issues for consideration in the suit.

(1) Was the suit barred by limitation?

(2) Was the story of surrender true?

(3) Had the plaintiffs got their alleged right, title and interest in the suit land?

(4) 	Was the story of possession and dispossession true?

(5) 	What relief, if any, were the plaintiffs entitled to?

7. In order to establish the respective claims of the parties, the plaintiffs examined as many as 8 PWs and the defendants examined 4 DWs. The learned Munsiff on consideration of the evidence on record and the facts and circumstances of the case decided the first issue against the plaintiffs who could not prove the factum of their possession and dispossession in the suit-lands. With regard to the 2nd issue about the story of surrender of the under raiyati of Eusuf Ali came to a finding against the plaintiff to the effect that the story of surrender of under-raiyati of Eusuf Ali could not be proved by the plaintiff beyond reasonable doubt and as such the story of surrender was not proved. He further decided the other issues against the plaintiffs and found no right, title, interest or possession of the plaintiffs in the suit-land and accordingly dismissed the suit on contest as against the defendant Nos. 1, 3 and 4 and ex parte against the rest by his judgment and decree dated 15.9.60. As against the said judgment and decree, the plaintiffs preferred an appeal being Title Appeal No. 276 of 1960 before the learned District Judge, Noakhali and the same was heard ultimately by the learned Subordinate Judge, Noakhali. The learned Subordinate Judge framed only one point for consideration as to whether the plaintiffs were entitled to get a declaration of their title and recovery of khas possession of the disputed lands mentioned in the schedule Ka and Kha of the plaint and thereafter on conclusion of the hearing of the appeal came to the following finding:

"It is the case of the plaintiffs that Eusuf Ali came over to his under-raiyati lands after taking settlement on the basis of Ext. 2(a) However, in view of the documentary evidences adduced on behalf of the plaintiffs there cannot be any shadow of doubt that the entire disputed lands came in khas possession of the plaintiffs. So the plaintiffs' case must be true. They had been dispossessed by the defendants since 7th Bhadra, 1358 BS." He also came to a finding to the following effect: So I think the plaintiffs case must be true that the defendant No. 1 and his mother went away to village Rasulpur in 1327 BS surrendering the lands of the under-rayati of Ext. 6(a) in favour of the landlords.

The learned Subordinate Judge further observed:

"As it appears that the entire disputed lands came in khas possession of the landlords, the plaintiffs case must be true that the daughters of Eusuf Ali orally surrendered their interest in favour of their landlords. Legally the interest of Mati Mia and Rahimunnessa did not pass under Ext. 4. So, the plaintiffs are entitled to a , declaration of their 16 annas share in the disputed lands, less the share of Mati Mia and Rahimunnessa. The share of Mati Mia and Rahimunnessa on calculation comes to 2 gandas of land. Hence, the plaintiffs are entitled to a declaration of their 16 annas title in the disputed lands, less 2 gondas of lands and they are entitled to a joint possession along with defendant Nos. 3 and 4."

8. He also found that the present suit was instituted within 12 years from execution of Ext. 4 dated 18.10.43. Thus on the above findings, the learned Subordinate Judge was pleased to allow the appeal in part on contest with cost and set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and decreed suit in part on contest with cost against the contesting defendants and ex parte against the rest by his judgment and decree dated 24.3.1962.

9. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree of the Court of appeal below, the contesting defendants preferred this second appeal and during the pendency of the appeal, appellant Mansur Ali having died his legal heirs and representatives were substituted as appellants in this appeal.

10. Mr. Faruque Ahmed with Mr. Abul Kalam, the learned Advocates appeared for the defendant appellants and Mr. Nikhilesh Datta, the learned Advocate appeared for the plaintiff-respondents.

11. Mr. Faruque Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the appellants after placing both the judgments of the courts below before me, firstly contends that the impugned judgment is not a proper judgment for reversal and as such this should be set aside. The contention of the learned Advocate for the appellants is that if Estafanama Ext. 4 is found to be genuine and valid and on that basis surrender of the suit lands in favour of the land-lords is found to have been done in accordance with law followed by delivery of possession, then the plaintiffs are entitled to get the relief as prayed for by a decree in the suit, but if the surrender of the suit-lands by the Estafanama Ext. 4 is found to be not genuine and in accordance with law but only followed by a delivery of possession in favour of the landlords, in that case the suit must fail and the judgment of the trial Court be upheld and that of the lower appellate Court be set aside. Therefore, in the instant case the main question is whether the Estafanama Ext. 4 was a genuine document and whether the surrender of the suit-lands was made and possession given by the heirs of late Eusuf Ali in accordance with law. Besides, it appears that the question of limitation also would depend upon the genuineness of the said Estafanama Ext. 4. The case of the contesting defendants was that Eusuf Ali, their predecessor-In-interest used to live in the house of his father-in-law Maniruddin as domesticated son-in-law at Batra and he all along was in possession of the suit-lands and on his death, his heirs also were in possession of the same.

12. Now, with regard to the Estafanama, the trial Court on consideration of the entire evidence on record found that it was not genuine and valid with regard to the question of possession, The trial Court came to a finding that the defendants were all along in possession of the suit-land, but the lower. appellate Court reversed the said finding of the trial Court and found that the surrender vide Ext. 4 was a genuine one and the same was followed by delivery of possession of the suit lands to landlords. Now, it is sericusly contended by the learned Advocate for the appellants that the trial Court on scrutiny of the evidence of both the sides held that there was no intention of the heirs of deceased Eusuf Ali to surrender the raiyati right in favour of the landlords and the alleged Estafanama was a false and fraudulent one. Firstly, for the reason that Sarbat Banu, the mother of defendant No. 1 who aIleged to have executed Estafanama on behalf of 2 other minors was an illiterate lady to whom the contents of the alleged Estafanama were not at all read over and explained in Bengali and now she has deposed in this suit as DW 4 and in her deposition, she has made her assertion and categorically stated that she did not surrender the suit-land and the alleged Estafanama was not read over and explained to her and as regards possessions she also stated that the defendants all-along were in possession and there was no delivery of possession in favour of the landlords after the so-called surrender. She has been corroborated by the evidence of other DWs, namely, DW 2 Fajool Mia and on the question of possession he has been also corroborated by other DWs. The lower appellate Court, it appears without considering the entire evidence on record with regard to surrender and possession of the suit lands and without adverting to the reasonings of the trial Court, wrongly found that Estafanama Ext. 4 to be genuine and found possession of the plaintiffs in the suit lands and illegally decreed the suit.

13. Mr. Nikhilesh Datta, the learned Advocate for the respondent, however, contends that in second appeal this court should not go to disturb any finding of facts He contends that the document Ext. 4 whether genuine or not is a finding of fact and, as such, the finding of the lower appellate Court with regard to the said document and possession should not be disturbed in the second appeal and as such the findings of the lower appellate Court should be upheld. With regard to the scope of section 100 and in support of his contention, the learned Advocate for the respondent has relied on a decision reported in 38 DLR (AD) 201 (Abdul Manna and others Vs. Bangladesh and another) and also on another decision in the case of Md. Naimuddln Sarder alias Naimuddin Vs. Abul Kalam Biswas @ Abul Kalam &another reported in 39 DLR (AD) 237, wherein it has been observed as follows:

"It is now well-established that the High Court Division can only invoke its jurisdiction under the said section (100) if there is any error of law or procedure committed by the first appellate Court and, as such, error has affected the merit of the decision, otherwise a finding of fact, however wrong it might appear, cannot be interfered with in second appeal."

In the same decision it has been further observed:

"If a finding is not based on evidence or if it is based on utter inadequacy of evidence on which no reasonable conclusion can be reached then interference therewith in second appeal is certainly justified."

And in the same decision it has been further observed:

"The plaintiff must succeed on his own case, and weakness of defendant's case is no ground for passing a decree in favour of the plaintiff."

14. Mr. Faruque Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the appellant however submits that the principles laid down in those decisions are not disputed, but the same are not helpful to the appellants in the present case. He has however cited another decision of our Appellate Division in the case of Md. Tabibur Rahman Molla Vs. Md. Sayedur Rahman & others reported in 36 DLR (AD) 48, wherein the scope of section 100 has been discussed and it has been held:

"Non-consideration of the material evidence by the lower appellate Court has exposed its finding to attack in second appeal."

The learned Advocate for the appellants also referred to another decision in the case of Maharuddin Fakir and others Vs. Jogendra Kishore Nag and others reported in 27 DLR 398, wherein it has been held:

"Non-consideration of the material evidence by the lower appellate Court has exposed its finding to attack in second appeal."

The learned Advocate for the appellants also referred to another decision in the case of Maharuddin Fakir and others Vs. Iogendra Kishore Nag and others reported in 27 DLR 398, wherein its has been held:

"The 'reasons for decision' in Order 41, rule 31(c) of the CPC makes it obligatory for the appellate Court to give his own reasons for his decision whether affirming or reversing the findings of the court below. The decision of the appellate Court must show that he had applied his independent mind into the points in dispute and has exercised his own discretion in deciding the points in dispute as a final court of facts. It is his duty to properly assess the evidence and advert to the findings arrived at by the court below and then either accept or reject them with his own reasonings. It is not that he has to write out an elaborate independent judgment, but the appellate Court judgment must be so self-contained that the findings of fact can be sustained upon a bare perusal of it."

15. Now, in the light of the above decisions, it may be seen whether the learned Subordinate Judge rightly reversed the finding of the trial Court on the question of surrender and possession of the suit-lands on proper consideration of the evidence on record and in accordance with law. The learned Advocate for the appellants raised another very material question as to whether the provisions of section 86 of the Bengal Tenancy Act have been complied within making the alleged surrender by Estafanama Est. 4. Section 86 of the Bengal Tenancy Act provides for making surrender.

It appears from a reading of the said section that in a case of surrender by the raiyat or under-raiyat there is provision for giving notice of his intention to surrender to the land-lords at least three months before making the surrender, and after the surrender by the raiyat or under-raiyat of his holding the landlord may enter on the same, either to let it to another tenant or take into cultivation himself and further when a holding is subject to an encumbrance secured by a registered instrument, or when there is an under raiyat on the holding or part thereof, the surrender of the holding shall not be valid unless it is made with the consent of the landlord and the encumbrancer or the under-raiyat, as the case may be.

Of course, sub-section 7 of the said section, 86 of the Bengal Tenancy Act provides:

"(7) Save as provided in sub-section (6) nothing in this section shall affect any arrangement by which a raiyat or under-riyat and his landlord may arrange for surrender of the whole or a part of the holding."

<u>16. It is therefore contended by the learned Advocate for the appellants that there is nothing on record to show that the said provisions of law were complied with in making the alleged surrender vide Ext. 4. He also contends that admittedly defendant No.2 was alleged to have executed the Estafanama on behalf of the 2 minors and even the appellate Court also found that there could not be a legal and valid Estafanama on behalf of any minor and, as such, he left out 2 gondas share of the suit-land from the decree passed in favour of the plaintiff. The learned Advocate for the appellants contends that it appears that there was a partial surrender of the holding which is not permissible without complying with the provisions of section 86 of the Bengal Tenancy Act and as such the alleged surrender vide Ext. 4 was not legal and valid in the eye of law. In this connection he has referred to a decision in the case Sademani Sarder Vs. Mohammadali Mollah & others reported in 12 DLR 239 where-in it has been observed:</u>

<u>"A part of the holding cannot be surrendered by some of the co-sharer tenants."</u>

17. In order to constitute a valid surrender of a part of a holding under the Bengal Tenancy Act, the provisions of section 86 of the Bengal Tenancy Act must be complied with and there must be an arrangement between all the tenants and all the landlords to that effect. But in case of surrendering the entire holding which is governed by section 86(1) of the Act no consent of the landlord is necessary.

<u>18. In this connection he has also referred to a decision in the case of Muhammad Sohrab Ali and others. Vs. Bazlur Rahman Mia and others reported in 1968 SCMR 341, wherein it has been held:</u>

<u>"A surrender is an yielding up of the term by the lessee to the person who has the right to re-enter, or in whom the immediate reversion expectant on the term is vested. In order to establish surrender by relinquishment of possession, the relinquishment must be in favour of the lessor, that is to say, a surrender may be implied from the fact that the lessee has permitted the lessor to re-enter and take over possession. It is, of course, not necessary that there must be, in every case, a physical taking over of possession but at least something amounting to a virtual taking over of possession must be proved, such as the lessee handing over the keys of the premises, to lessor, or the doing of some other act which would indicate a present intention to yield up the tenancy in favour of the lessor. To make out a case of abandonment, non-user must be accompanied by some other circumstance evidencing an intention to abandon. Similarly, for surrender also a mere relinquishment of the tenancy is not enough. A relinquishment without the making over of possession is not a valid surrender. The intention of the lessee must be the guiding factor is such case. Though this intention may be inferred from his actions A lease-hold interest being a heritable and, a transferable interest could be transferred to another person and, as such, the mere transfer of such an interest could not amount to an abandonment or relinquishment of the tenancy."</u>

19. Now, from the above decision, it is very clear that to make a valid surrender, the provision of section 86 of the BT Act has to be complied with and along with the surrender of holding, there must be delivery of actual possession in favour of the landlords. Now, it is the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellants that the trial Court in consideration of the entire evidence on record both oral and documentary came to a finding that the defendants were all along in possession since before the alleged Estafanama and the plaintiffs failed to prove their possession in the suit-land. The trial Court discussed the evidence of all the PWs and DWs and also other documentary evidence but the lower appellate Court has not considered the evidence of most of the witnesses and particularly the evidence of the DWs and also he has not come to any specific finding as to possession of the parties, particularly with regard to the alleged Estafa nama and it shows that he had not followed the procedure in case of reversing a decision of finding on consideration of the evidence and other materials on record and as to the Estafanama there is nothing on record to show that the provision of section 86 of the BT Act has been complied with in making the alleged surrender vide Estafanama Ext. 4. It appears that he has failed to advert to the reasonings of the trial Court in reversing its findings on the question of surrender by Ext. 4 and also possession in the holding at the relevant time.

20. I have considered the above submissions of the learned Advocates visa-vis the facts of the case and the evidence on record and the provisions of law and I am of the view that the learned Subordinate Judge has committed error of law as well as of procedure in reversing the findings and decision of the trial Court. It further appears that he has misread some relevant documents and misconstrued the same namely, Exts. A-2B, the kabuliyat and wrongly relied on the same in coming to a finding that the Estafanama was genuine one and consequently there has been a gross miscarriage of justice.

21. In view of the above, I therefore find much fore in the arguments of the learned Advocate for the appellants and hold that the impugned judgment of the court of appeal is not a proper judgment of reversal and the same cannot be sustained in law and on facts and is liable to be set aside. It appears that the decision of the trial Court is quite sound and correct, being based on correct appreciation of law and the materials on record.

22. In the result, the appeal is allowed and the impugned judgment and decree of the court of appeal below are set aside and those of the trial Court are upheld, and restored. The cross-objection is accordingly dismissed.

In the facts and circumstances of the case there will be no order as to cost. Let the lower courts records be sent down immediately.

End.

full_judgment:
Shahabuddin, J.-This appeal is directed against a decree of the Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Faridpur dated 31.3.61 passed in T.S. No. 10 of 1969 declaring the plaintiff's title to the suit land. Hence the defendant has come in this appeal.

2. Case of the plaintiffs as set out in their plaint is that plaintiffs Nos. 8.18 along with proforma defendants Nos. 2.5 were proprietors of revenue paying estate comprised in touzi No. 7414 of Faridpur Collectorate. This touzi has been recorded in R. S. Khatian No. 509 of mouza Bhennabari. There are three under tenures of this touzi and they have been recorded in R.S, Khatians Nos. 510, 512 and 514 of the same mouza Plaintiffs No. 7-18 also held the under tenure recorded in one of them, namely R.S. Khatian No. 510 directly under the estate and their names have been recorded as under tenure holders therein. Plaintiffs Nos. 1-6 were not owners of the estate but they have possessed the under-tenure interests in the other two under-tenures recorded in Khatians Nos. 512 and 514 under the plaintiffs Nos. 8 to 18. These plaintiffs claimed to have been in actual possession of the land and some of them have got their homestead therein. On 13.7.59 they came to learn that the touzi was sold to one Kali Krishna Chakraborty in auction for arrears of government revenue on 22.6 55. No notice of the sale had been served upon them but a notice was found to have been issued to one dead proprietor namely, Bicharan Biswas, predecessor in interests of plain tiffs Nos. 10, 11 and 12. The sale was therefore invalid and the under tenures were never annulled. On the wholesale acquisition of rent receiving interest from April, 156 the plaintiffs were recorded in the S. A. Khatians as tenants-in-possession under the government, But defdt. No. 1, Ammullaya Ch. Kundu claiming that the auction purchaser Kali Krishna Chakraborty had been his benamdars filed an objection petition under section 19 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 to the Revenue Officer, Gopalganj and got his name recorder as tenant in possession under an order dated 13.7.59. This order of the Revenue Officer got no basis whatever and the plaintiffs title to the land was not affected thereby. Hence they filed the suit praying that title of plaintiffs NO.9 be declared in 'K' schedule land representing R.S. Khatian No. 512, that of plaintiffs, Nos. 1-5 in 'Kha' schedule land representing R.S. Khatian No. 514 and that of plaintiff Nos. 7.18 in ‘Ga’ schedule land representing R. S. Khatian No. 510.

3. The suit was contested by defendant No. 1 who claimed that the revenue sale was held in his favour and the ostensible purchaser was his mere benamder and that by filing an application to the Deputy Collector he got his name' mutated in Register D of the Faridpur Collectorate. He contended that this suit was not maintainable on a number of grounds. The suit, he contender was hit by section 33 of the Bengal Revenue Sales Act, (Act XI of 1859) since it was not bid within one year from the date of confirmation of the sale on grounds "declared and specified" in a prior appeal to the Commissioner. Further, he contended, the suit was hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act since he bad lack delivery of possession under a fertilize e of possess issued by the Collectorate on confirmation of the sale on 17 9.55 and annulled all the encumbrances, such as the under tenures, by serving notice of annulment, by beat of drum and also by filing a Rent Suit against one Keshab Ch. Das, a sub-tenant under the plaintiffs. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the evidence both oral and documentary held that the sale was invalid having been held in contravention of the provisions of the Sales Act, 1859 and that even if the sale were not invalid the plaintiffs' Interests in the under tenures of the touzi were not affected thereby since these under tenures were never annulled under section 37 of the Sales Act. It was further held by the learned Subordinate Judge that the suit was not for setting aside the sale but was for a declaration of the plaintiffs' title which remained unaffected by the sale. On these findings he decreed the suit.

4. Mr. B.B. Roy Chowdhury the learned advocate appearing for the defendant, appellant has assailed the impugned on a number of grounds. He has contended that the suit, though declaratory in form, is actually a suit challenging the sale and as such the suit is hit by section 33 of the Sales Act. Secondly, the suit, he contends is hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act since the purchaser has been in possession of the suit land on the basis of the writ of possession issued by the Collector followed by annulment of the encumbrance. Mr. Chowdhury has assailed the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge that the encumbrances were never annulled. He has further challenged the finding that the sale was invalid.

5. There is no dispute that plaintiff’s No. 8.18 along with proforma defendants No. 2-5 were or orbiters of the touzi No. 7414 and they were also holders of the under-tenure directly under themselves. We have already found that the touzi was recorded in R.S. Khatian No.509 and that its under-tenures have been recorded in R.S. Khatian Nos. 510 51, and 51 4. Plaintiffs Nos. 8 to 18; along with plaintiff No. 7, have been recorded as the Molders of the under tenure in R. S. Khatian No, 510 and the other plaintiffs have been recorded as holders of the under-tenures

In R S Khatian Nos. 512 and 514. Defendant No. 1 led evidence to show that the touzi was sold for arrears of revenue in public auction held by the Collector of Faridpur on 22.6.55 ostensibly to one Kali Krishna Chakratorcy and that Kali Kristina Chakraborty was his benamder Later on, defendent No. 1 got his name mutated in the Register-D of the Collaborate as the purchaser. This question of benami purchase has not been seriously challenged in this suit except a suggestion that the ostensible purchaser having left the country, defdt. No. 1 tried to trans-plant himself into the position of the purchaser. The sale was confirmed on 13.9.55 and no appeal against it was preferred to the Commissioner under section 2 of Act VIII of 1868, The Act, it may be noted, is also called the Bengal Land Revenue Sales Act (1968) and it has amended section, 25 of the Sales Act of 185). Mr B B. Roy Chowdhury has argued that this suit is actually a suit against the sale in question though in the garb of declaration. There is no dispute that if it is a suit challenging the sale in question it will be hit by section 33 of the Sales Act. This section provides "No sale for arrear of revenue shall be annulled by a court except upon grounds of its having been made contrary to the provision of this Act and then only on proof that the plaintiff has sustained substantial injury by reason of the irregularity complained of and no such sale shall be annulled upon such ground unease such ground shall have been declared kind specified in an appeal made to the Commissioner under section 2 of Act VIII of 1838."

The learned Subordinate judge has observed that the sale was invalid and as such there was no necessity to get this sate set aside by an appeal to the Commissioner. The sale was to be held on 20.6.55 according to the sale notice, but it was not held on that day; it was held or 22.6.55 without any reason having been shown for shifting the date. The learned Subordinate Judge observed that the sale was thus held by disregarding the provision of section 20 of the Sales Act. Again, 25% of the purchases money was paid by the purchaser on the date of sale but the balance, which was to be paid positively within the thirtieth day from the sale, was paid after two months. This contravened the mandatory prevision of section 23 of the Sales Act, the learned Subordinate Judge further observed Mr. B.B. Roy Chowdhury has contended that these contraventions of the provisions of sections 20 & 23 of Sales Act are mere irregularities, and even if they were illegalities they did not render the sale 'void'; at best the sale was voidable and hence remedy against it lay only in an appeal to the Commissioner under section 2 of Act VIII of 1868 in support of this contention, he has relied upon a decision of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, Raja Govinda Lal Roy Vs. Ramjanam Mister and . others, 20.1.A 165 In that case a suit was filed against a sale without first following the procedure of section 33 of the Sales Act and it was contended that the provisions of section 33 need not be followed as the sale was held in contravention of the provision of the Sales Act. This contention was rejected and it was held that even a sale held in contravention of the Sales Act was required to be set aside under the provision of section 33. Their Lordships held:

"A sale is a sale made under the Act XI of 1859 within the meaning of that Act when it is a state for arrears of government revenues held by the Collector or other officers authorised to hold sales under the Act, although it may be contrary to the provisions of the Act either by reason of some irregularity is publishing or conducting the sale, or in consequence of some express provision for exemption having been directly con traveled."

6. Mr. S.S. Halder, the learned Advocate appearing to support the impugned decree of the learned Subordinate judge does not dispute this proposition of law as to a sale held illegally, but he has submitted that the learned Subordinate judge himself did not, in fact, give much importance to the question of the alleged illegality of the sale since the learned Subordinate judge held that even if the sale were valid the plaintiffs' interest as under-tenure holders were not affected thereby. This leads to the question of annulment of the under-tenures of the touzi. Mr. B.B. Roy Chowdhury has referred to the certificate of possession dated 17.9.55 issued by the Collector on confirmation of the sale. Admittedly, possession delivered under this certificate is a symbolical possession since, in the touzi there were under-tenure holders who were in actual possession. Mr. B.B. Roy Chowdhury contends that symbolical possession from the Collector on confirmation of a sale amounted to actual possession and as such the defaulting proprietors stood dispossessed thereby and that they could not have filed the suit for mere title without praying for recovery of possession in support of this contention he has relied upon a decision of this Court in the case, Almaj Khatun Vs. Ejahar Mir, 8 DLR 82. In that case a suit was filed for having a revenue sale set aside by deposit of the government dues. Earlier the Collector .had refused to set aside the sale by accepting the said depot sit under the provision of section 37 (A) of the Sale Act. The suit was dismissed as It was found to have been hit by section 33 of the Sales Act in that the ground taken in the suit for setting aside the sale had not been declared and specified in an appeal to the Commissioner under section 2 of the Act, Villa of 1868. But in that case a passing reference was made to the question of the effect of a symbolical possession on confirmation of a sale and it was held "symbolical" possession obtained in a suit for ejectment in respect of a plot in the occupation of a tenant-judgment debtor is effective to terminate the possession of such tenant." We fall to understand how this observation in will help the appellant before us. Symbolical possession is a good as actual possession against a judgment debtor, and this principle of law was finally settled as far back as in 1917 by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in a case reported in 23 CWN 37. But in the case before us the under-tenure holders were not judgment debtors so as to lose their actual p3ssession by a certificate of possession issued by the Collector on sale of the superior interest, the touzi. it Is true that when a sale for arrear of revenue is confirmed and a certificate of possession is issued to the purchaser, the certificate of possession amounts to actual possession against the defaulting proprietors But the defaulting properties tors before us were also the under tenure holders a separate class of tenants in Khas possession. The Collector's Certificate of possession did not terminate their possession automatically.

7. Mr. B.B. Roy Chowdhury has relied upon section 37 of the Sales Act of 1859 to show that the interests of the under tenure holders were also affected by the certificate of possession. Section 37 provides that a purchaser of revenue paying estate purchases it free from all encumbrances and be is entitled to avoid and annul all under tenures excepting certain interests which have been specifically mentioned in that section. These interest are "instimrarl" or "mukarrarl" tenures which have been held at a fixed rent from the time of the permanent settlement; tenures existing at the time of settlement at rent which is not liable to enhancement except under law; talukdari and other similar tenures created since the time of settlement and held immediately under the proprietors of the estates; and leases of lands whereon dwelling houses, man features, or other permanent buildings have been created or whereon garden, plantations have been made. The plaintiff’s tenures do not come under any of these four "exceptions", which are known as "protected interest" though in respect of some of the plots therein they claimed to have held the tenures since the time of the permanent settlement. No evidence has, however, been led in support of the claim. Their main contention is that their under tenures were never annulled and that they continued in possession as under-tenants in spite of the sale and that is why they were recorded as tenants-in-possession on the whole-sale acquisition of rent receiving interests. Mr. B.B. Roy Chowdhury has contended that the under tenures were "encumbrances" which stood annulled on the sale of touzi but the purchaser also took positive steps to annul them by various means, such as by serving notice upon the under tenures and by filing a rent suit against a sun tenant of the under tenants. We do not think that Mr. Chowdhury contention of automatic annulment of an under tenure is tenable. The question as to annulment of under tenures and encumbrances in consequence of a sale came up for consideration before the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of Turner Morrison & Co. Vs. Monmohan Chowdhury reported in 36 CWN 29 and the decision given therein ill an authority on the subject. For better application of the question raised before us we propose to discuss the law and facts Cal that case.

8. In that case a revenue paying estate known as "Taraf Asad Mosed Khan" was sold for arrears of revenue in 1913. Directly under the estate there was a taluk named "Taluk Rommohan" and under the taluk there was an under tenancy record in favour of the defendants of that suit, Turner Morrison & Co. The purchaser had filed a suit in 1923 before the learned Subordinate Judge, Chittagong for ejecting the sub-tenants claiming that the sub tenancy good automatically annulled in consequence of the sale of the estate in 1913. The learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the suit holding that the sub-tenancy was not affected by the sale since neither sub tenancy nor the taluk above it was annulled under section 37 of the Sales Act. In appeal the High Court held that in view of the confirmation of the sale followed by writ of possession the taluk which was an "encumbrance" stood annulled and consequently, the sub-tenancy under the taluk met the same fate. Their Lordships of the Privy Council rejected this proposition of law as given by the High Court and held that an under tenure is not an 'encumbrance' but it is a different thing altogether, and that the High Court fell into an error by drawing an analogy between the encumbrances defined in the Sales Act and that defined in the Bengal Tenancy Act 1885. Their Lordships held:

"High Court held that a taluk is an encumbrance. Some confusion has perhaps been introduced by reference to the corresponding provision of the Bengal Tenancy Act but the two Acts are not in pari-materia and the differences between them are considerable. No doubt under the Bengal Tenancy Act an intermediate tenure would be an "encumbrance" sees sec, 159 and sec. 161 where an encumbrance is defined. But in then Lordships' opinion it is not so under section 37 of the Revenue Sales Act of 1859. This section draws a clear distinction between encumbrances and under tenures. Encumbrances are wiped out by the sale; in the case of under tenures, the purchaser is only entitled to void and annul them and on doing so that is upon exercising his option to annul, he can eject the under tenants  Unless and until the taluk is annulled it continues: and the talukdar becomes the under-tenant of the purchaser and the tenants holding under him are not affected by the change of proprietorship There is no private of contract between them and the purchaser, and the latter cannot either claim rent from them or eject them so long as he allows the taluk to continue f he purchaser could, no doubt sue for possession of the holding joining both the talukdar and the talukdar's tenants. The institute of such suit would be an effective election to annul the taluk and the joinder o& the persons in actual possession would be in accordance with the ordinary procedure".

In view of this settled principle of law the contention of automatic annulment of the plaintiffs, under-tenure holders before us falls to the ground Mr. Chowdhury then concentrated his arguments on the defendant's claim that he had actually emoted the under-tenures by overacts which are going to be examined absently.

9. Defendant No. 1, the purchaser has stated that after confirmation of the sale he sent a notice by registered post to the plaintiffs stating that the under-tenures stood annulled. He produced four postal receipts Ext-C series in support of this contention. The plaintiffs denied having received any such letter. Plaintiff No. 1 who purportedly a knowledge the receipts denied his signatures thereon. No attempt was made by the defdt No. I to get the signatures examined by an expert. On the contrary, he withdrew all these receipts from the lower court but never produced them thereafter. Defendant No. 1 did not say when he had sent this notice under the receipts, Ext. C Series nor did the receipts contain any date of issue. Date of issue of the alleged notice is material in this case, for hardly a period of six months after confirmation of the sale bad passed when the purchaser's proprietary interest in the touzi extinguished by the wholesale state acquisition. If the notice of annulment had been issued after the extinction of his interests it was totally useless. A postal receipt invariably shows the date of issue. Absence of the date of issue of the receipts Ext-C series and their subsequent disappearance raise question as to their genuineness. Excepting the oral evidence of Defdt No. 1 there is no evidence of service of notice upon the plaintiffs. As to announcement in the locality by beat of drums it is again defendant No.1, the purchaser, who alone deposed to this effect. No beater of drum was examined nor even named by defendant No .1. In these circumstances the claim of annulment by notice of beat of drum is found to have been rightly rejected by the learned Subordinate Judge.

<u>10. The other evidence of annulment on which Mr. B. B. Roy Chowdhury has given emphasis is a certificate of sale issued on 13.10.57 in a rent suit being Rent Suit No. 24 of 1957 of the Court of Munsif Gopalgzonj. It shows that defendant No. 1, as a purchaser of the touzi, had filed the suit claiming rent from one Kesab Das who was a tenant of the plaintiffs Nos. 8 to 18 in respect of a sub-tenancy recorded in R.S Khatian No. 516 directly under R.S. Khatian No. 510. These plaintiffs were made proforma defendants in that rent suit since they were under-tenure holders above the sub-tenancy. The plaintiffs have contended that no notice of the rent suit was served upon them or upon the principal defendant and that it was after suit instituted for the purpose of creating evidence as to annulment. They have produced an application, Ext. H (1) showing that the exparte decree passed in the Rent Suit was sought to be set aside on the ground of no service of notice. We need not detain ourselves to this allegation as to no service of notice but will proceed on the assumption that such a rent suit was filed and was also decreed exparte and see whether his decree in the rent suit followed by it is execution can help the purchaser in any way. Mr. Chowdhury has contended that institution of such a suit against a sub-tenant claiming rent within the knowledge of the sub tenants' immediate landlords will he insufficient evidence that the annulment was complete in support of this contention he has relied upon a decision of the Calcutta High Court in 50 CWN. 37, in that case a touzi was sold and thereafter a rent suit was filed against some of the under-tenure holders and it was held that the certificate of possession issued in the rent suit in which the holders of the intermediate superior tenure holders were also parties was sufficient proof of election of option" of the purchaser for annulment. It was held:</u>

<u>"When the purchaser of a superior interest becomes entitled to annul an intermediate tenure, a demand of rent directly from an under tenant in the presence of the tenure holders constitutes an effective election to annul the tenure.</u>

<u>We have hardly anything to differ from this decision, but we are clearly of the view that this decision does not help the appellant before us in any way. For, a decree in a rent suit like the one as referred to shows only the intention of the purchaser of a superior interest to annul the under-tenure and a certificate of possession is the rent-suit terminates the tenure only from the date of the institution of the suit. It does not give any retrospective effect to the termination of the tenure from the date of sale. That is why it was clearly stated in the judgment:</u>

<u>"The certificate proceeding however, could not effect annulment earlier than the date of its institution which was the 15th of April 1936 corresponding to the 2nd Baisakh, 1343. It follows that the plaintiff’s claim for the year from 1339 to 1342 must in any event fail"</u>

<u>The sale in that case was held as already referred to above in 1932 and the suit for rent was filed in 1936 and the decree of the rent suit terminated the tenure from 1936 and not from 1932. In the case before us even if the Rent Suit No. 24 of 1957 was a genuine case against a sub-tenant of the plaintiffs, tenure holders, it terminated the tenure from September, 1957 when the suit was filed but by this time the purchaser lost all his right, title and interest in the land because of acquisition of his rent receiving interests with effect from 14th April 1956.</u>

<u>11. In summarizing the points discussed above we are clearly of the view that the revenue sale held on 22.6.55 terminated the proprietary interests of the plaintiffs in the touzi but it did not automatically wipe out the under-tenures in the touzi. The sale only rendered these under-tenures voidable at the option of the purchaser. He was to exercise his option by institution of a suit, by serving a notice upon the under-tenure holders, by collection of rents or by some other overt act clearly indicating his intention to annul. This view of ours has got direct decision of this reported in 16 DLR, 582. The purchaser is not found to have annelid the under-tenures by any of these methods within the short time he got support from a previous Court in a similar case from confirmation of the sale to the extinguishment of his interest in the touzi the under-tenants having remained in possession till the 14th April, 1956, they were rightly recorded as tenants in possession of the land in the Khatian. But when this entry in the Khatian was altered by the Revenue Officer u/s. 19 of the State Acquisition Act on 13.7.57 showing the purchaser as tenant-in-possession their title was threatened and hence the filed the suit for declaration of their title It is therefore, not a suit against the sale to the Touzi. The suit is in proper form and is found to have been rightly decreed.</u>

12. Before we conclude we like to observe that some additional evidence was sought to be adduced in this Court by this appellant and There was an order of this court that this question would be discussed at the time of hearing. The intended evidence is judgment of a subsequent suit, being Title Suit No. 112 of 1960 in the court of Munsif, Faridpur which was passed on 15th July 1961 that is, three months after impugned judgment and decree before us. That was suit for a declaration that the revenue sale in question was fraudulent one. The suit was dismissed. Mr. Roy Chowdhury does not go to that extent as to say that this subsequent decree in a suit between the same parities will operate as a res judicator in the present suit which was decided earlier. But he has drawn our attention to the fact that the sale in question was found to be a genuine one in a separate suit. Be that as it may in view of our findings as stated above, the intended additional evidence does not help the appellant any way whatever. In the result, in repeat is dismissed on contest with costs and the impugned decree of learned Sub ordinate judge is affirmed.

M.H. Rahman. J. -- I agree.

End.

caseno:
Writ Petition No. 532 of 1980 and
Writ Petition No. 143 of 1981
lawyer:
Mozammel Huq ----- For the petitioner in both the rules. 
B. N. Chowdhury with Parimal Chandra Guha -----For respondent in both the Rules.
parties:
M/s. Chowdhury Sons Ltd (in Writ Petition No 532/1980) ----- Petitioner 

Group Superintendent, Chowdhury & Sons Ltd. (in writ petition No. 143/1981 ----- Petitioner 
Vs. 
Chairman, Labour Court at Chittagong & ors ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Abdul Wadud Chowdhury, J.—These two Rules arise out of two application under Article 102 of the Constitution of People's Republic of Bangladesh and are directed against the order passed by the Chairman, Labour Court, Chittagong in industrial Dispute Case Nos. 104 of 1979 and 86 of 1979 allowing the respondent No. 2's applications under section 34 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance and setting aside the order dated 22.10.79 passed by the Managing Agent of the Tea Estates and directing the Managing Agent to allow the Respondent No. 2 to resume their duties in Baramashia Tea Estate. In these two rules same questions of law and facts are involved and as such both are taken up together and disposed of by one judgment.

2. The applicants before the Labour Court i.e. the respondent No. 2 in both the petitions were working in Baramashia Tea Estate. The Respondent No. 2/of Writ petition No. 532 of 1980 was working as clerk for a pretty long time. The said Tea Estate originally belonged to Pakistan-Plantations and subsequently vested in the Government of Bangladesh. The Government of Bangladesh subsequently disinvested the said Tea Estates and Bengal Mines Development Corporation purchased it. The petitioner Company is the Managing Agent on behalf of Bengal Mines Development Corporation as regards the said Baramashia Tea Estate. Suddenly the Group Superintendent of the petitioner company at Chittagong issued order of transfer of the respondent No. 2 to Karnaphuli Tea Estate. The respondent No. 2 submitted representations on 31.10.79 for allowing him to continue to work in Baramashia Tea Estate. The respondent No. 2 in Writ Petition No. 532 of 1980 fell sick and prayed for sick leave. But in the meantime the Group Superintendent issued orders releasing the respondent No. 2 from the service of the Baramashia on 30.10.79 directing him to report at Karnafuly Tea Estate. The Respondent No. 2 due to illness could not join these duties and the Group Superintendent issued another letter asking him to submit explanations for alleged misconduct and unauthorised absence. Explanation was submitted by the respondent No. 2 on 15.11.79. In the meantime after recovery from sickness the respondent No. 2 submitted representation on 10th December, 1979 to allow him to resume duty in Baramashia Tea Estate but the Group Superintendent refused to allow him to resume his duty at Baramashia Tea Estate and directed him to report for duty in Karnafully Tea Estate.

3. So far as the Writ petition No. 143 of 1981 is concerned the facts are to the effect that the respondent No. 2 was a permanent employee of Baramashia Tea Estate. He was intially appointed as a daily rated worker in 1964 and in 1966 he became an Assistant Electrician and from 1977 he became a monthly rated employee. He is the General Secretary of Chittagong Cha Bagan Sramik Union, a registered Trade Union and as such incurred the displeasure of the employer for his Trade Union activities. He is a permanent employee of Baramashia Tea Estate and there is no rule transferring the respondent No. 2 from this garden to some other garden belonging to a different person. It is stated that Karnafully Tea Estate is owned by M/s. Abdul Qader Chowdbury Sons Ltd. and Baramashia Tea Estate is owned by M/s. Bengal Mines Development Corporation. As such the owners of these two concerns being different these two gardens were managed by the same managing agent the transfer of the respondent No. 2 of both the writ petitions to different garden owned by a different person cannot be said to be legal. In that view of the matter respondent No. 2 in both the petitions filed two application before the Labour Court, Chittagong under section 34 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969 and contended that their transfers from Baramashia Tea Estate to Karnafully Tea Estate were illegal and as such not maintainable The Managing Agent contested the cases before the Labour Court. Their case were to the effect that the application under section 34 of the Industrial Relation Ordinance 1969 were not maintainable and totally misconceived. They contended further that the respondents could be transferred from one garden to another garden under the same management. The petitioner here was the managing agent of both the estates and both the gardens were being managed by one group superintendent under the same managing agent and as such the managing agent was the employer of both the respondents No. 2 of the writ petitions and these transfers from Baramashia to Karnafuli Tea Estate were valid and legal, and this could not be challenged before the Labour Court.

4. The Labour Court allowed the case of the respondent No. 2 of both the cases and set aside the orders of transfer and release of the respondent No. 2 of both the cases from Baramashia and directed the Managing Agents to allow the first party to resume their duties in Baramashia Tea Estate. The Labour Court held that the workers may be transferred from one department to another, one section to another or one plantation to another within the management of the same employer at the discretion of the Manager of the employer provided, that no worker shall be reduced in grade or pay. But in the present cases Baramashia Tea Estate and the Karanafuly Tea Estate are two different plantations belonging to different persons and as such the transfer could not be said to be valid. He also held that though the Managing Agent of the said two gardens were the same they could not exceed their limit by transferring an employee of one garden belonging to one owner to a garden belonging to another owner by virtue of their being the common Manager of both the gardens. As against this order the Managing, Agents have come up with these applications and obtained the present rules.

5. Mr. Mozammel Huq, the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the petitioner and Mr. B.N. Choudbury with Mr. Parimal Chandra Guha, learned Advocates appeared for the respondent No. 2 Mr. Mozammel Huq, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the applications before the Labour Court under section 34 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969, were not maintainable as section 34 was not applicable in the fact and circumstances of the present cases. He argues that if the respondents so liked they could have come up under section 25 of the Employment of Labour (Standing Order) Act and not under section 34 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance. He has also submitted that the petitioner was the employer of the respondent No.2 of both the petitions and being the Managing Agent of both the Tea Estate and as such employer transferred them from Baramasbia Tea Estate to Karnafully Tea Estate and said orders of transfer were valid and legal and as such the Labour Court erred in law in allowing the application under the Industrial Relations Ordinance. 1969 and directing the petitioner the Managing Agents to allow the respondents to joint the Baramashia Tea Estate. We have considered the facts and circumstances of the case. In our view the judgment and order passed by the learned Labour Court in both the cases are legal and do not suffer from any illegality. So far as the question of non-applicability of section 34 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969 we find that the application before the labour court under section 34 were maintainable because of the fact that under section 34 workers could apply to the Labour Court for enforcement of any right guaranteed by law.

6. In the present cases the respondent No. 2 being employees of the Baramashia Tea Estate owned by one owner was transferred to Karnafully Tea Estate which belonged to another owner. The law is to the effect the employee could not be transferred from employment of one employer to the employment of another employer without the consent of the employee. Moreover, there is implied contract between the owner and the employee as regards service in the garden and in that view of the matter the transfer of the respondent No. 2 from Baramashia Tea Estate to Karnafully Tea Estate belonging to different owner cannot be said to have been done with lawful authority. With regard to the contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioners that the employee had remedy under section 25 of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965 it appears that provisions gives out the cases under which the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act would be applicable. But the respondent No: 2's case is not covered by the provisions of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, as such the contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner cannot be sustained and we find that section 34 applies to the cases of the respondent No. 2 and it could not be said that the petition under section 34 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance before the Labour Court was not maintainable. Mozammel Huq then argued that the petitioner being the employer of the respondent No. 2 it was their right to transfer them to any garden under their management at different plantations. But the petitioners who were the employees of Baramashia Tea Estate being vested with the right with regard to their service in the ownership of Bangladesh Mines Development Corporation could not be transferred to the Tea Estate of M/S. Abdul Qader and Sons Ltd. without the agreement amongst the staff and the owners. In the instant cases there was no such agreement between the staff and the owners. In that view of the matter of the contention of the learned advocate for the petitioner that being common managing agent they could transfer an employee from one garden belonging to one owner to another garden belonging to another owner cannot be sustained.

In that view of the matter we do not find any substance is these two rules. These two Rules are, therefore discharged. In the facts and circumstances of the case there will be no order as to costs.

Sultan Hossain Khan J.-I agree.

End.

lawyer:
Syed Refaat Ahmed for Mahmudul Islam, Advocate—For the Petitioner. 
ABM Nurul Islam with Maksuda Akhtar and Farah Mahmuda, Advocates—For the Respondents.
parties:
Shafiqul Islam Patwari (Md) ----- Petitioner
vs.
Administrator of Waqfs, Government of Bangladesh and another ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Matin J : This Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 28-9-93 as contained in Annexure-A issued by the Administrator of Waqfs, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh Dhaka purporting to appoint a new Managing Committee in place of present Mutawali of "Afsar and Saira Khatun Waqfs Estate" shall not be declared to have been passed without any lawful authority.

2. The facts of the case, in brief, are that Afsaruddin and Saira Khatun Waqf Estate was created on 20-12-1943 by Md. Afsaruddin and his wife Mst. Saira Khatun by registered Waqf Deed No. 15303. The waqf deed provided for the appointment of Mutawalli  and in accordance with Clause 3 of the Waqf Deed the first Mutwalli of the Waqf Estate was Md. Afsaruddin. After his death his wife Mst. Saira Khatun was the Mutwalli. On her death his daughter Begum Faizunnessa was appointed Mutawalli and thereafter Begum Faizunessa's son Abdus Sattar was appointed Mutawalli. On 15-10-80 during the lifetime of Abdus Sattar his son Golam Haider was appointed Naib Mutawalli in order to assist him. While he was the incumbent Mutawalli of the said Waqf Estate Abdus Sattar passed away on 1-1-92 and the position of the Mutawalli fell vacant. Thereafter the petitioner filed an application on 17-5-92 for appointing him as Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate before the Administrator of Waqf, the Respondent No. 1. The respondent No. 1 directed the Inspector of Waqfs, Greater Comilla District to investigate and submit a report. The Inspector of Waqf submitted a report on 13-9-92. Thereafter, on 23-9-92 the Naib Mutawalli Golam Haider applied to respondent No. 1 to be appointed as Mutawalli in place of his deceased father Abdus Sattar. Thereafter, a further inquiry was conducted by the Assistant Administrator of Waqfs, Chittagong Division who filed a report on 30-3-93.

3. On consideration of the reports mentioned above the respondent No. 1 appointed the petitioner as Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate vide his order dated 8-4-1993 and since then the petitioner has been continuing as the Mutawalli. The respondent No. 3 filed an application on 6-4-93 to the Respondent No. 1 praying for appointing him as Mutawalli but the said application was rejected on 14-4-93. Thereafter on 19-4-93 one Shamsul Haque Patwari, a brother of respondent No. 3, and others made an application to respondent No. 1 for staying operation of the order dated 8-4-93 appointing the petitioner as Mutawalli and for appointing respondent No. 3 as Mutawalli of the said Waqf Estate. Thereafter, a group of about 21 persons who are the family members of the Waqif and the stipendiaries of the Waqf Estate made a representation to the Respondent No. 1 praying for continuation of the petitioner as the Mutawalli. The respondent No. 1 thereafter by its order dated 28-9-93 cancelled the appointment of the petitioner as Mutawalli and directed appointment of a Managing Committee of 7 persons including the petitioner and respondent No. 3 and making the respondent No. 2 its Chairman for Administration of the said Waqf Estate.

4. Being aggrieved by the order of cancellation of the appointment of the petitioner as Mutawalli and ordering appointment of Managing Committee in his place vide order dated 28-9-93 the petitioner moved this Court and obtained the Rule.

5. Mr. Syed Refaat Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that the impugned order dated 28-9-93 as contained in Annexure-(A) cancelling the appointment of the petitioner as Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate having not been made on any of the grounds stated in section 32 (1) of the Waqf Ordinance and having been passed on extraneous ground that the majority of beneficiaries of the Waqf Estate do not support the claim of the petitioner has been passed without jurisdiction and is liable to be declared as having been made without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect. The learned Advocate further submits that the order directing appointment of a Managing Committee of the Waqf Estate is wholly without lawful authority inasmuch as section 34 sub-section (3) does not contemplate appointment of a Managing Committee in cases other than of Shrine, Dargah, Imambara or other Religious Institution and in the instant case no shrine or Imambara or other religious institution is involved.

6. Mr. ABM Nurul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 3, does not challenge the legal position in respect of sections 32 and 34 of the Waqf Ordinance 1962 but submits that in view of the Annexures annexed to the supplementary affidavit filed by the Respondent No. 3 the Respondent No. 1 should have appointed respondent No. 3 in place of the petitioner.

7. Heard the learned Advocate, perused the writ petition and the affidavit-in-oppositin and the annexures annexed thereto.

8. It appears from Annexure-B to the writ petition that the Waqf Estate was created by Afsaruddin Patwari and Saria Khatun vide registered deed of waqf executed on 20-12-43.

9. Annexure-C to the writ petition is an application filed by the petitioner to the respondent No. 1 on 17th May, 1992 praying for appointment as Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate.

10. Annexure-D to the writ petition is the inquiry report filed by the Waqf Inspector dated 12-9-92 recommending the appointment of the petitioner as Mutawalli.

11. Annexure-E to the writ petition is another application by one Colam Haider praying for appointing him as Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate.

12. Annexure- E (1) is another inquiry report dated 30-3-93 filed by Assistant Waqf Administrator Chittagong Division recommending appointment of the petitioner Md. Shafiqul Islam as the Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate.

13. Annexure-F is the order of appointment of the petitioner as Mutawalli dated 8-4-93.

14. Annexure-G is an application of the Respondent No. 3 dated 6-4-93 praying for appointing him as Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate.

15. Annexure-H is another application filed before the respondent No. 1 by Md. Shamsul Hoque Patwary and others praying for staying the operation of the order dated 8-4-93 and for appointing respondent No. 3 as the Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate.

16. Annexure-I to the writ petition is an application made by Alhaj Mofizuddin Patwari and 20 others to the respondent No. 1 supporting the case of Md. Shafiqul Islam Patwari as Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate and praying for eviction of the unauthorised persons from the land of the Waqf Estate.

17. Annexure-D dated 12-9-92 is a report of the Waqf Inspector and Annexure-E (I) is another report by Assistant Administrator of Waqf Chittagong Division dated 30-3-93. The respondent No. 1 directed investigation about the candidature of the petitioner as Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate and after due inquiry Officers reported to the respondent No. 1 recommending the appointment of the petitioner as Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate and consequently the petitioner was appointed as Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate vide order dated 8-4-93 by the Respondent No. 1.

18. On perusal of the Annexure-A, the impugned order dated 28-9-93, it appears that respondent No. 1 found that the enquiry reports supported the candidature of the petitioner as Mutawalli. But the respondent No. 1 cancelled the appointment of the petitioner as Mutawalli only because the majority of the beneficiaries of the Waqf Estate allegedly do not support the claim of the petitioner. It further appears that the respondent No. 1 directed appointment of Managing Committee of 7 members including this petitioner and the respondent No. 3.

19. The learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner has referred to section 32 (1) of the Waqf Ordinance which runs as follows:

"32 (1) Notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this Ordinance or in any other law for the time being in force, the Administrator may, on his own motion or an application of any person, remove a Mutawalli-

(i) for breach of trust, mismanagement, malfeasance or misappropriation; or

(ii) for any act of the Mutwalli causing loss of waqf property or affecting the proper administration, control or preservation of the waqf; or

(iii) if the Mutwalli has been convicted more than once under section 61 of this Ordinance, or

(iv) if the existing mutawalli is found unsuitable, incompetent, negligent or otherwise undesirable; Provided that no such order for removal of a mutawalli shall be made without giving him an opportunity of being heard."

20. On a consideration of section 32 sub-section (1) as quoted above it appears that the Administrator may, on his own motion or on application of any person, remove a mutwalli on any ground mentioned above.

<u>21. But it appears that the petitioner has been removed as Mutawalli not on any of the grounds enumerated in sub-section (1) of section 32 of the Waqf Ordinance which has been mentioned above but that the majority of the beneficiaries did not support his claim as Mutawalli. We hold that the petitioner has been removed on extraneous ground not contemplated by section 32, sub-section (1) and as such the same has been done without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect.</u>

22. The learned Advocate again referred to section 34, sub-section (3) which runs as follows:

"34(3) The Administrator may manage the waqf property taken over by him under sub-section (1) through any officer subordinate to him or by an agent or official mutawalli or, if he considers necessary, by appointing a managing committee in the case of shrine, dargah, imambara or other religious institution."

<u>23. On perusal of the Waqf Deed it is clear that this Waqf Estate does not relate to any shrine, dargah or imambara or other religious institutions and, as such, the order directing appointment of a Managing Committee in place of the petitioner is beyond the scope of section 34 (3). Besides, it appears that a Managing Committee can be appointed only when the Administrator takes over the management of the Waqf Estate and after notification in the official Gazette about taking over. In this case the Administrator has not taken management nor any notification has been published in the official Gazette to the effect that the Administration of the management has been taken over by the respondent No. 1 and, as such, the order directing appointment of a Managing Committee by the impugned order has been made without lawful authority and in violation of section 34(3) of the Waqf Ordinance.</u>

In view of section 32 (1) and section 34 (3) as referred above we are of the opinion that the respondent No. I had no authority to cancel the appointment of the petitioner as Mutawalli only on the alleged ground that he was not supported by the majority of the beneficiaries of the Waqf Estate and the order directing appointment of a Managing Committee in place of the petitioner is wholly unauthorised and is hereby declared as having been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

24. Mr. ABM Nurul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 3, however, submits that respondent No.3 filed an application for appointing him as the Mutawalli and Shamsul Hoque Patwari and 7 others filed a petition before the respondent No. 1 praying for appointing respondent No. 3 as Mutawalli on the ground stated therein as will appear from Annexure-1 to the supplementary affidavit. He has drawn our attention to Annexure-3 to the supplementary affidavit dated 26-11-93 showing that Thana Nirbahi officer, Motleb, Chandpur sent a report with names of the proposed member of the Managing Committee to the respondent No. 1

25. The learned Advocate further referred to Annexure-3 of the supplementary affidavit showing that the petitioner was involved in Motlob PS Case No. 7 dated 15-8-93 under sections 147/148/149/323 325/379 BPC. The learned Advocate submits that though the respondent No. 1 acted illegally in directing the formation of Managing Committee in place of the petitioner he should act as directed by this Court to consider these Annexures and pass necessary orders in respect of appointment of the Mutawalli of the Waqf Estate in question. In view of our findings in respect of the impugned order dated 28-9-93 as contained in Anne- ure-A to the writ petition we hold that any direction as prayed for by the Advocate of the respondent No. 3 in the facts and circumstances of this case will be unwarranted and accordingly we find no substance in the submission of the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 3.

26. In view of the discussions and findings made above the impugned order dated 28-9-93 as evidenced in Annexure-A to the writ petition cancelling the appointment of the petitioner as Mutawalli and directing formation of the Managing Committee in his place is hereby declared as having been made without any lawful authority and is, of no legal effect.

This Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Rafiqul Huq with Shariful Islam Khand and Nitai Roy Chowdhury, Advocates — For the Petitioners.
Kaiseruddin Ahmed, Deputy Attorney-General — For Respondent No. 1. AF Hasan Arif, Advocate — For Respondent No. 4.
parties:
Mohsin Hossain (Md) and others ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Mozammel Hoque J : This Rule has arisen out of an application under Article 102 of the Constitution calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the purported acquisition of the land measuring 4. 79 acres recorded in SA Plot Nos. 24, 25 and 42 of mouja Samir, Police Station formerly Tejgaon, now Gulshan, District Dhaka, lying unused, should not be declared to be without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

2. It is stated in the application that in LA Case No. 33 of 1958-59 several acres of land were purported to have been requisitioned for the Master Plan of Gulshan Model Town and in that LA Case the CS Plot Nos. 24, 25, 26, 42 and 43 measuring more or less 4.79 acres of land were also included. It is the specific case of the petitioners that they became the owners of the suit land by virtue of several registered deeds and since then they have been possessing the same and before them their predecessors-in-interest also possessed the suit land. It is their further case that since for about last 37 years land in question remained unused for which it was allegedly acquired, the acquisition in question was not acted upon and the aforesaid land was not required for the purpose for which it was acquired. Since 1984 there was consistent policy of the Government that the unused acquired land for a long period would be returned to the owners even without consulting the requiring body and in pursuance of that policy of the Government several hundreds of acres of land in different areas, which were not used for the purpose, were directed to be returned to the original owners and, as such, the petitioners being the owners of the land are entitled to get back the aforesaid land in question as the same remained unused for last 37 years.

3. It is the case of Respondent No. 4, the Rajdhani Unnayan Kartripakkha that in LA Case No. 33 of 1958-59 the land in question was taken over by RAJUK by Gazette Notification for the purpose of the Master Plan of Gulshan Model Town and since the land in question vested to RAJUK and RAJUK is the owner since Gazette Notification dated 23-6-60, the property in question cannot be returned to the owners. It was the further case of respondent No. 4 that the original owners were given compensation and, as such, they had no right to transfer the same to the present petitioners. Since the present petitioners are purchasers in the year 1989, they had no locus standi to file the writ petition inasmuch as the property vested to the requiring body RAJUK in the year 1960.

<u>4. In the background of the case as stated above let us see first the documents and papers which they have annexed with the writ petition as well as with the affidavit-in-opposition and the affidavit-in-reply. Annexures-A to D of the writ petition are the photo copies of the certified copies of different deeds of transfer by which the present petitioners are claiming to be the owners of the land in question. Annexure-E is the Gazette notification purported to have been issued on June, 23, 1960 under sub-section (4)(f) of section 93A of the Town Improvement Act wherein the SC Plot Nos. 24, 25, 26 and 42 have been included. Annexure-F is the proceeding of the inter-Ministerial meeting held on 15-11-1984 with Mr MA Huq, the Minister for Land Administration and Land Reforms in the Chair in connection with the land acquisition cases in Kathalbagan and Kalabagan area of the Dhaka City. In that meeting decision was taken that the lands which were not used for such a long time in the aforesaid area should be released in view of the fact that for a long time the requiring body failed to use the aforesaid land. Annexure-F(I) is a map which shows that he suit land, namely, Plot Nos. 24, 25, 26, 42 and 43 remained vacant and the same was not used till today by RAJUK. Annexure-G is the report of the Executive Engineer in respect of the possession of the unused lands which were purported to be acquired by LA Case No. 6 of 1948-49. Annexure-H is a letter issued by the Ministry of Land directing the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka, to give information to the Ministry with regard to the present land. The Deputy Commissioner was also directed to inform the Ministry as to whether the lands in question were acquired for any organisation. Further, whether the requiring body had used this land in question. Further, it was directed to inform the Ministry that if the lands in question were not used, then who had been possessing the suit land and whether as unused land, the requiring body had returned the same to the owners or not.</u>

5. This information was asked from the Deputy Commissioner by the Ministry in pursuance of the letter of the petitioner vide Annexure-H(I). Annexure-H(3) is the copy of the map of the area in question.
